title: The Contribution of Mergers and Accretion to Dark Matter Halo Assembly: An Excursion Set Theory Approach
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures
summary: We study the relative contributions of mergers and accretion to the assembly of dark matter haloes within the framework of Excursion Set Theory (EST). We extend a variance-discretized merger-tree algorithm, which recursively reconstructs all branches of a complete merger tree and introduces a merger-ratio criterion for distinguishing mergers from accretion. The method is validated by comparing the resulting progenitor distributions with the analytical conditional first up-crossing distribution, showing excellent agreement over a wide range of halo masses and redshifts. We find that the accretion contribution depends strongly on the adopted merger-ratio threshold. For large merger ratios ($MR=0.1$--$0.25$), accretion accounts for up to $\sim70\%$ of the mass growth of massive haloes, whereas including all resolved mergers ($MR=10^{-6}$) reduces the accretion contribution to $\sim40\%$. These values are in good agreement with previous N-body simulation results. The accreted mass exhibits a nearly self-similar distribution in the mass-redshift plane, with the dominant contribution arising from progenitors in the range $10^{-3}M_0 \lesssim M \lesssim 10^{-1}M_0$ and predominantly at $0.5 \lesssim z \lesssim 2$. Our results demonstrate that EST-based merger trees provide an accurate and computationally efficient framework for investigating halo assembly and quantifying the relative roles of mergers and accretion in hierarchical structure formation.

title: MOSS III: MeerKATs view on the galaxy populations in two massive galaxy clusters
summary: The MeerKAT Observations of the Saraswati Supercluster (MOSS) is an ongoing project attempting to study the radio and optical properties of the core region of the Saraswati supercluster (z = 0.28) and will eventually entail a full survey of the entire supercluster region. Here we use radio catalogs from previous deep pilot MeerKAT L-band (1.28 GHz) observations (angular resolution of 8 arcsec) of the core region of the Saraswati supercluster. The region hosts two galaxy clusters representing distinct environments: The most massive cluster Abell 2631, and the second most massive cluster ZwCl2341, that is significantly more dynamically active. The deep radio catalogs of these clusters were combined with spectroscopic redshifts (mainly from DESI DR1 and SDSS DR16) and optical photometry catalogs of the cluster member galaxy source population. We use these redshifts together with the 1.4GHz MeerKAT flux densities to derive the dust-free star-formation rate (SFR) and evaluate various trends in the radio SFG and AGN galaxy populations. We find that the actively merging cluster ZwCL2341 has an increased star-forming galaxy population compared to A2631 with up to 4 times more star-forming galaxies. When looking at SFG-related radio processes we see s enhanced SF-related activity in ZwCL2341 with SF-related radio processes dominates entirely over AGN-related radio processes. This suggests that dynamically active environments associated with cluster assembly, such as mergers, have enhanced SF radio-activity and increased SFG (both radio and non-radio) galaxy population compared to lesser active systems.

title: Kinetic Theory of the EFTofLSS : A Halo-Based Approach
comment: 44 pages, 22 figures
summary: The Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure (EFTofLSS) provides a coarse-grained description of the non-linear gravitational clustering of dark matter, in which the effects of short-scale physics are encoded in an effective stress tensor and a set of counterterms. In this work, we develop a framework to investigate the physical origin of these counterterms by relating the effective stress tensor to the dynamics of individual dark matter halos in cosmological N-body simulations. We find that halo accretion contributes to the trace of the halo-based effective stress tensor, contributing to the background pressure and effective sound speed, while anisotropic accretion generates the traceless part, consequently contributing to the shear viscosity. For the halo population with $M_\mathrm{vir}>10^{12}\,M_\odot/h$, we find that halos account for $\sim\!95\%$, $\sim\!85\%$, and $\sim\!70\%$ of the full box background pressure, effective sound speed, and shear viscosity, respectively, depending on the EFT cutoff scale. The contributions to the counterterms are dominated by cluster-scale halos, $M_\mathrm{vir} \sim 10^{14} - 10^{15}\,M_\odot/h$ and halos with larger inflow rates, supporting an interpretation in terms of accretion-driven, out-of-equilibrium dynamics. Our results provide a short-scale, kinetic-theory interpretation of the EFTofLSS counterterms and establish a framework for connecting the properties and dynamics of short-scale structures to physics-informed priors for large-scale cosmological observables.

title: A Nonlinear General Implicit Runge-Kutta Integrator for Multifluid Charged Dust and Gas
comment: Submitted to ApJS
summary: Charged dust in magnetized gas is subject to aerodynamic drag and the Lorentz force, both of which can be difficult to model numerically in a fluid simulation where their characteristic timescales are shorter than the timestep set by the Courant condition. We present a two-stage general implicit Runge-Kutta (GIRK) source integrator for multifluid charged dust coupled to an ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) gas, implemented in the open source GPU-accelerated quokka code. Drag and Lorentz forces are advanced together in one implicit source update, avoiding errors in the terminal drift that can arise when the two forces are advanced in separate substeps. The timestep is compared with a drag-Lorentz timescale to select between resolved and stiff branches. The resolved branch uses Gauss-Legendre coefficients, while the stiff branch uses a coefficient set designed to recover the terminal drift set by the drag-Lorentz balance. We also allow the dust stopping time and charge-to-mass ratio to depend on the evolving state, evaluating them separately at the two implicit stage states and solving the resulting nonlinear stage equations by Picard iteration. The source update conserves total gas-dust momentum, and its computational cost scales linearly with the number of dust species. Tests reproduce the expected drag damping and terminal drift, confirm the predicted gyromotion amplitude and phase errors, demonstrate accurate treatment of state-dependent source coefficients, and recover the expected wave, shock, and instability dynamics in dusty MHD flows.

title: GroArnold: A Framework for Constructing Action-based Models for Triaxial Galaxies and Dark Matter Halos
comment: Our key results: see the logic flow of the code in Fig. 1; see the universal $f(J)$ function in Eq. (13) and its fitting demonstration in Fig. 8
summary: Action-based distribution functions $f(\mathbf{J})$ provide a powerful description of stellar systems. Consequently, the construction of physically accurate and dynamically stable $f(\mathbf{J})$ for galactic components has emerged as a key challenge in the field. In this study, we present GroArnold, a computational framework designed to construct analytical $f(\mathbf{J})$ expressions for axisymmetric and triaxial galaxies and dark matter halos. The framework integrates modules for $N$-body initial condition generation, $N$-body simulation, angle--action variable estimation, and distribution-function fitting into a unified workflow. It supports a wide range of density profiles and kinematic properties, and is uniquely designed to generate stable $N$-body models for user-specified galactic systems, with the aim of obtaining an $f(\mathbf{J})$ that approximates a dynamically stable and physically consistent state. To this end, we extend the triaxial Stäckel Fudge method of the TACT code, implemented in our Nbody-TACT module, to enable action estimation directly from $N$-body gravitational potentials. GroArnold provides a robust and flexible tool for deriving numerically empirical, explicitly analytical distribution functions for user-specified galaxies or halos, thereby facilitating a wide range of practical $f(\mathbf{J})$-based modeling applications. In addition, it serves as a powerful tool for investigating the dynamics of realistic triaxial galaxies and halos beyond the scope of traditional spherical or axisymmetric models. We assessed the accuracy of the output $f(\mathbf{J})$ by comparing its predicted spatial and velocity distributions with those of the input $N$-body snapshot, and confirmed that it provides a reasonably accurate representation of the input. The code is modular, publicly available, and designed to support future extensions and adaptations.

title: TNGC-SIDM I: Evolution of massive cluster mergers under the self-interacting dark matter paradigm
comment: 24 pages, 23 figures. To be submitted to A&A. Comments welcome
summary: Merging galaxy clusters provide an ideal laboratory for testing the self-interacting nature of dark matter. In this paper, we present a pilot study of magnetohydrodynamical cosmological zoom-in simulations of two cluster mergers selected from TNG-Cluster, with $M_{\rm 200c} \sim 9\times10^{14}~M_\odot$ and $M_{\rm 200c}\sim 2\times10^{14}~M_\odot$. The simulations are performed with both standard collisionless cold dark matter (CDM) and self-interacting dark matter (SIDM), assuming an isotropic, velocity-independent cross-section of $σ_{\rm T}/m_χ= 1~\rm cm^2~g^{-1}$, with an additional $0.5~\rm cm^2~g^{-1}$ run for the low-mass system, and the mass resolution and galaxy formation model are unchanged from TNG-Cluster. We show how dark matter self-interactions produce an isothermal core in the dark matter halo, generate unique substructures in the intracluster light, and introduce variation in the multi-wavelength observables of the intracluster plasma. Using these simulations, we test the validity of observational probes for dark matter self-interactions in cluster mergers. We find that the shock-to-shock separation shows similar evolution in the self-interaction models tested here, providing a reference for distinguishing the $\sim100-200~\rm kpc$-scale difference in halo separation induced by self-interactions. Moreover, the dark matter halo centroid of the main cluster in the massive cluster merger is offset from the brightest cluster galaxy by as much as $\sim20~\rm kpc$, larger than the offset in the sub-cluster. This offset persists beyond 4 Gyr after the first pericenter passage. Our results indicate that sample selection plays a key role in testing the possible self-interacting nature of dark matter using cluster mergers, and that double radio relic cluster mergers and massive clusters with evidence of an ancient major merger offer a promising testbed for this purpose.

title: Extrapolating Collisional Rate Coefficients for Molecules of Astrophysical Interest Using Neural Networks
summary: State-to-state rate coefficients for inelastic molecular collisions are essential inputs for non-local thermodynamic equilibrium radiative transfer models, yet their computation using quantum scattering methods is prohibitive for large molecules and highly excited rotational states. We investigate the ability of artificial neural networks to extend existing datasets of collisional excitation rate coefficients without performing additional scattering calculations. A multilayer perceptron model was trained using molecular quantum numbers, level energies, energy gaps, and kinetic temperature as descriptors, and optimized on logarithmic rate coefficients. The model was tested on diverse collision systems ranging from simple diatomic molecules (CO, SiO) to open-shell species (SO), small asymmetric tops (H$_2$O, SO$_2$), and complex organic molecules (benzonitrile and vinyl cyanide) colliding with H$_2$ molecules or He atoms. Extrapolations were performed toward higher rotational levels, higher temperatures, and combinations of both. For most systems, predictions of rate coefficients involving previously unseen rotational states yielded mean error factors between 1.1 and 1.5, with the dominant rate coefficients generally reproduced more accurately than weaker transitions. Temperature extrapolations proved particularly successful, while combined extrapolations in temperature and rotational levels remained accurate to within a factor of two in most cases. The prediction quality depends on the interplay between dataset size, temperature range, molecular complexity, and the presence of clear collisional propensity rules. Overall, the approach demonstrates that machine learning can provide a practical route to extending collisional datasets for astrophysical applications, especially for large molecules for which additional quantum-scattering calculations are computationally demanding.

title: Signature of GW from the Hidden Sector in light of the Recent LZ Event
comment: 17 pages, 6 captioned figures, 2 tables
summary: The LZ collaboration has recently reported a single nuclear-recoil event at $E_R=248\pm23_\text{stat}\pm23_\text{sys}$ keV, observed in a 2.84 tonne-year exposure with a local significance of $3.4σ$, pointing towards an inelastic dark matter (DM) interpretation. We explain this event within a gauged $U(1)_X$ hidden-sector model, spontaneously broken by a singlet scalar whose vacuum expectation value (VEV) gives rise to: \textit{(i)} gauge boson mass, \textit{(ii)} a small Majorana mass for the vector-like singlet fermion, the DM candidate, charged under the new symmetry, which splits the fermion into two pseudo-Dirac states (mass splitting proportional to the scalar VEV) thus resulting in a purely off-diagonal vector current, \textit{(iii)} the frequency and the amplitude of the GW signal arising from the hidden sector symmetry breaking via first-order phase transition (FOPT). The symmetry-breaking scale thus provides a multi-messenger probe connecting terrestrial direct-detection kinematics at the LZ and early-universe FOPT thermodynamics while obtaining thermal DM relic abundance. We delineate the viable parameter space compatible with the LZ event, correct relic density, and detectable GW signals in the low frequency regimes at future interferometers like $μ{\rm ARES}$ and THEIA while satisfying existing cosmological, astrophysical, and terrestrial bounds.

title: Atomic hydrogen in $z=0$ galaxies in the COLIBRE simulations
comment: Submitted to MNRAS
summary: We present an overview of the properties of atomic hydrogen (HI) in galaxies at redshift $z=0$ in the COLIBRE cosmological galaxy formation simulations. COLIBRE directly simulates the multi-phase interstellar medium (ISM) and includes new methods to follow radiative cooling to $\approx 10\,\rm{K}$, non-equilibrium chemistry coupled to dust, and dust formation, growth \& destruction. We focus on the $(200\,\rm{cMpc})^3$ volume with resolution elements of $2\times 10^{6}\,\rm{M}_{\odot}$. No HI properties informed the calibration of model parameters and yet we find very good agreement with the observed $M_{\star}$-$M_{\rm{HI}}$ relation, the HI mass and velocity width functions, the HI mass-size relation, and (baryonic) Tully-Fisher relations, albeit with some mismatches at the extremes of the galaxy population. HI surface density profiles are realistic, except at large radii around massive ($M_{\star}\gtrsim 10^{10}\,\rm{M}_{\odot}$) galaxies where we find a population of possibly spurious circumgalactic HI clouds, whose abundances and masses decrease, however, with increasing mass resolution). Using smaller simulations to vary some of the uncertain model parameters, we find that the main scaling relations are at most mildly affected, although this may not extend to detailed HI morphokinematics. Convergence across mass resolution levels a factor of $8$ higher and lower is good: the median HI mass and HI `occupation fraction' as a function of halo mass, and the HI mass function, are remarkably stable, although the highest resolution model overproduces HI sources by a factor of $\approx2$ at $M_{\rm{HI}}\gtrsim 3\times 10^{9}\,\rm{M}_{\odot}$. Upturns in the low-mass and low-velocity slopes of the HI mass and velocity width functions with potentially subtle observational signatures are predicted.

title: A radio counterpart of the local little-red-dot J092359+415736
comment: accepted for publication in A&A Letter
summary: Little red dots (LRDs) are compact red sources at z>~4. Broad lines suggest accreting black holes, yet radio and X-ray measurements are usually weak. Local LRDs allow multi-frequency, multi-epoch radio studies that are inaccessible at high redshift. We search archival radio images for a counterpart to the local LRD J092359+415736 at z~0.323, quantify its long-term radio variability, and identify the plausible origin of the radio emission. Flux densities at the optical position are measured in FIRST, LoTSS, RACS, VAST, and VLASS products spanning 0.144-3.0 GHz and 1994-2024. A compact 144 MHz counterpart is detected at 42sigma in LoTSS, coincident with the Gaia position, and is recovered in FIRST, RACS, VAST, and VLASS. LoTSS and ASKAP give a spectral index alpha ~ -0.30 +/- 0.11. The source varies on multiple timescales: FIRST at 1.4 GHz (1994) is a factor of ~2.6 below ASKAP (2021-2024) and below the extrapolated LoTSS-ASKAP spectrum, indicating long-term brightening over 26 yr; the 3 GHz flux density rises by 2.3sigma between VLASS epochs 2.2 and 3.2. A star-formation-only origin would require ~200 Msun/yr, against an unobscured H-alpha upper limit of 3.3 Msun/yr, implying an extreme obscured starburst. Ordinary radio supernovae and tidal disruption events are strongly disfavoured by the luminosity and 30-yr recovery, while refractive scintillation would itself require an ultracompact nuclear emitter. The persistent radio counterpart is best explained by accretion onto the central black hole. Among the three radio-detected local LRDs, this source is intermediate in luminosity and the only one with reported multi-year variability, adding a temporal dimension to the radio diversity of the class.

title: WaveDM.jl: An Adaptable Simulation Framework for Dynamics of Baryonic and Wave Dark Matter on Galaxy Scales
comment: Accepted. Comments welcome
summary: We present WaveDM$.$jl, an open-source Julia package for high-performance simulations of wave dark matter dynamics on galaxy scales, with a design philosophy centered on extensibility and adaptability. The code solves the time-dependent Schrödinger--Poisson equation (SPE) using a pseudo-spectral Fourier method. The spectral solver is tightly integrated with N-body gravitational force solvers, enabling simultaneous evolution of wave dark matter and baryonic components in galaxy-scale simulations. WaveDM$.$jl unifies shared-memory, distributed-memory, and GPU execution within a multi-level parallelization framework, enabling the same computational workflow to scale from single-node to multi-node computing environments without requiring major code changes. To further facilitate user-friendly galaxy-scale simulations, the package provides a dedicated toolbox that integrates flexible initial condition generators, trajectory lookback, tidal force calculations, and real-time visualization. Beyond astrophysical applications, the code's modular architecture and general nonlinear Schrodinger framework enable cross-disciplinary studies such as nonlinear optics and cold-atom physics. The code is open source and available on https://github$.$com/JuliaAstroSim/WaveDM$.$jl.

title: Astrophysical Parameters of 5056 Open Star Clusters from Bayesian Nested Sampling with PARSEC Isochrones
comment: 23 pages, 11 figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS. Posterior chains: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23349618 ; code: https://github.com/oplevne/ocnsfit
summary: We present a homogeneous catalogue of ages, metallicities, distances, and reddenings for 5056 open clusters in the Unified Cluster Catalogue (UCC), derived uniformly from Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3) colour-magnitude diagrams via Bayesian nested sampling with PARSEC isochrones. Unlike previous large-scale catalogues, metallicity is fitted as a free parameter for every cluster rather than fixed or adopted from the literature: where available, Gaia XP spectrophotometric metallicities inform the fit (1201 clusters), while the remaining clusters are constrained by broad priors from Gaia parallaxes and the Schlegel-Finkbeiner-Davis dust map. No cluster is anchored to an external open-cluster parameter catalogue, and no per-cluster manual intervention is applied. A fit-quality metric, $η_{\rm fit}$, identifies 3807 clusters (75 per cent) with reliable colour-magnitude solutions, spanning ages of 0.004-5.9 Gyr and distances out to 17 kpc. We validate the resulting parameters against six literature catalogues and, more critically, against independent high-resolution spectroscopic metallicities from OCCAM DR19: for 132 clusters in common we find a median absolute deviation of only 0.054 dex ($-0.021 \pm 0.132$ dex mean offset), comparable to the intrinsic systematic uncertainty of isochrone-based metallicities. As a direct consequence of this fidelity, the radial metallicity gradient recovered from our XP-informed clusters ($-0.064$ dex kpc$^{-1}$) steepens towards the spectroscopically calibrated value ($-0.079$ dex kpc$^{-1}$) for the highest-quality subset - demonstrating that a purely photometric pipeline, built without reference to spectroscopy, recovers a physically meaningful abundance scale. The full catalogue and posterior chains are publicly released.

title: Deep X-ray View of a Distant Protocluster Anchored by a Quasar at $z=6.63$: No Evidence for Enhanced X-ray AGN Activity
comment: 32 pages, 12 figures. Accepted for publication in ApJ. The X-ray source catalog and merged images are available at https://zenodo.org/records/21945827
summary: Whether dense environments accelerate SMBH growth during cosmic reionization remains uncertain because X-ray constraints on $z>6$ protoclusters are rare. We analyze $\sim865$ ks of Chandra observations of J0910-0414 quasar field, a massive protocluster at $z=6.63$. We construct a catalog of 251 X-ray sources and search for AGN among 21 spectroscopically confirmed members, excluding the central quasar. This is the first systematic X-ray AGN census in a $z>6$ protocluster; none of the members is individually detected. Stacking all members ($\sim17$ Ms total exposure) yields no significant signal and limits the average rest-frame 2-10 keV luminosity to $\langle L_{\rm 2-10~keV}\rangle\leq9.54\times10^{42}~\rm erg~s^{-1}$. The null result gives a central 90% Jeffreys upper bound of $f_{\rm AGN}<0.09$. After accounting for the spatially varying sensitivity, the field Compton-thin X-ray luminosity function predicts $N_{\rm exp,field}=0.0356$ AGN in the surveyed volume. Assuming the overdensity profile of AGNs in this protocluster is the same as that of galaxies determined by Wang et al. (2024), the expected AGN count becomes $N_{\rm exp}=0.131$. Zero detections then imply a one-sided 90% upper limit of $η_{\rm rel}<17.5$ on any additional X-ray AGN enhancement beyond that associated with the galaxy overdensity. Although $η_{\rm rel}<17.5$ permits more than an order-of-magnitude enhancement, the data show no significant excess of X-ray-detectable AGN in J0910-0414 protocluster. The present X-ray data may miss heavily obscured, intrinsically X-ray-weak, or intermittently accreting SMBHs; the non-detection therefore does not rule out AGNs among the member galaxies.

title: The Forgetful Black Hole: Memory Burden and Hysteresis in Hawking Evaporation
summary: The memory-burden scenario of black hole evaporation proposes that Hawking emission may become increasingly suppressed as maintaining stored quantum information becomes dynamically costly. In this work, we revisit this scenario and investigate the conditions under which information retention can produce a genuine dynamical burden. We derive general scaling conditions for incremental memory accumulation at a fixed fractional mass loss and establish a conditional no-go result: entropy-suppressed, zero-mean deposits with subextensive integrated correlations cannot produce an order-one luminosity modification through unamplified accumulation and bounded feedback. We identify three essential requirements for dynamical memory: a record of the past must be written, retained, and coupled back to subsequent evaporation. We illustrate these requirements with concrete toy models that exhibit either a prolonged but finite black hole lifetime or an asymptotically approached finite-mass state (an effective remnant). We further distinguish kinetic-memory, thermodynamic-memory, and spectral-memory sub-categories of possible memory-burden mechanisms. In particular, we demonstrate that an independently evolving memory variable can generate evaporation-accretion hysteresis, such that a black hole returning to the same mass may possess a different retained memory and consequently a different luminosity. This history dependence may have implications for primordial black hole phenomenology. Finally, we briefly discuss the possibility of "merger rejuvenation", in which black hole mergers reorganize or reset the effective memory state.

title: Scalar-Assisted Growth of Supermassive Black Holes: Boson-Mass Windows and Observational Constraints
comment: 23 pages, 10 figures
summary: We study a phenomenological cosmological model of black-hole growth in which a finite baryonic reservoir and a bosonic scalar cloud feed the black hole simultaneously. The baryonic component accretes through an Eddington-like channel, while the scalar cloud transfers mass through an effective quasibound-state decay rate. Evolving the system directly in redshift within a flat $Λ$CDM background, we scan over $μ$, $M_0$, $M_{c,0}$, and $M_{b,0}$ to assess whether scalar-assisted accretion can accelerate the formation of $10^9M_\odot$ supermassive black holes. We find that the scalar contribution is highly selective in parameter space. For the mass scales explored here, scalar transfer is most efficient for $μ\sim10^{-19}-10^{-16} \mathrm{eV}$, producing rapid cloud depletion and significantly earlier black-hole growth, while outside this interval the evolution remains mainly baryonic. More generally, this efficient window reflects a preferred range of the dimensionless coupling $α=μM_{\rm BH}$ and therefore shifts approximately as $μ\propto M_{\rm BH}^{-1}$. Comparison with observed quasar masses and luminosities instead favors lower boson masses, broadly around $μ\sim10^{-21}-10^{-20}\mathrm{eV}$. These results are not necessarily in tension, since the boson mass that maximizes early growth depends on the characteristic black-hole mass and evolutionary stage. This separation between dynamical efficiency and observational compatibility leaves open complementary roles for different bosonic mass scales in supermassive black hole growth and dark-matter phenomenology.

title: Substructure-enhanced Collisional Relaxation in Stellar Systems
comment: Our key results: see the dependence of the enhanced collisional relaxation on the positional-space fractal dimension in Fig. 4; see the positional-space enhanced ratio in Fig. 6; see the velocity-space enhanced ratio in Fig. 13
summary: Two-body collisional relaxation in stellar systems is conventionally estimated using the classical Chandrasekhar theory, in which a subject star is assumed to be embedded in a homogeneous medium of field stars and their velocity distribution taken to be isotropic and Gaussian. Real stellar systems, however, can exhibit pronounced spatial and kinematic substructures. We investigate how such substructures -- particularly the non-classical spatial inhomogeneity -- modify the two-body diffusion coefficient. We retain hyperbolic two-body encounters but generalize the encounter calculation by integrating explicitly over the spatial distribution $n(\mathbf{r})$, while evaluating the velocity contribution from the full distribution $f_v(\mathbf{v})$. This yields a separable tensor expression for the diffusion coefficient. We find that spatial substructure produces the dominant enhancement. The enhancement of the diffusion coefficient increases systematically as the effective fractal dimension $D_{\rm frac}$ decreases, $\log ζ_r(D_\text{frac}) \sim \left(1-D_\text{frac}/3\right)^q$ with $q \approx 4.28$. For the observationally motivated case with $D_{\rm frac}\approx 1.5$, the enhancement is moderate, whereas substantially lower fractal dimensions produce much larger enhancements. In contrast, the anisotropic, power-law-tailed, and fractal-like velocity distributions modify the diffusion coefficient only by factors of order unity. Our representative substructured model yields enhancement ratios $ζ_r\simeq3.45$ and $ζ_v\simeq1.33$ when the measured particle-number trends are extrapolated to $N=10^{11}$, corresponding to an overall enhancement of $ζ\simeq4.6$. Therefore, within the two-body encounter framework and the commonly used separable distribution functions, the enhanced collisional relaxation still has little impact on the mean-field nature of typical galactic systems.

title: Forecasting a Cosmological 21 cm Stacking Detection with Early HIRAX Data
comment: 30 pages, 10 figures, 1 table. Submitted
summary: Post-reionization 21 cm intensity mapping provides a powerful technique for efficiently mapping the Universe on large scales. The Hydrogen Intensity and Real-time Analysis eXperiment (HIRAX) is a compact and highly redundant radio interferometer designed to exploit this technique. We present a forward modelling pipeline for forecasting a statistical detection of the cosmological 21 cm signal with HIRAX through cross-correlation with an external source catalogue. We simulate the cosmological signal using the halo model and propagate it, together with Galactic and extragalactic foreground emission and instrumental noise, through a model of an early-stage 36-dish HIRAX array configuration. We generate simulated visibilities, apply delay-domain foreground filtering, and construct cross-correlation-ready ringmaps for an observing time of 120 days with a single zenith pointing over the frequency range from 700 to 800 MHz, covering approximately 3547 deg$^2$ of the sky. We investigate the prospects for an early statistical signal detection by stacking these ringmaps at the known three-dimensional positions of sources from an overlapping external survey. Specifically, we quantify how delay-domain foreground filtering, the number of stacking sources, catalogue completeness, and source redshift uncertainties affect the detection significance. We find that redshift precision is the most critical requirement: while spectroscopic redshifts with $σ_z / (1+z) \sim 0.001$ preserve a significant stacking signal even under realistic foreground filtering and substantial catalogue incompleteness, photometric redshift uncertainties of $σ_z / (1+z) \sim 0.01$ strongly suppress the signal for realistic delay cutoffs. Applying the framework to a Euclid-like spectroscopic galaxy sample, we recover a minimum signal-to-noise ratio of 11 for our most conservative delay cutoff of 100 ns.

title: EMRIs in Kerr Spacetime: The Role of Inclination Diffusion
comment: 21 pages, 14 figures, 1 table. Comments are welcome
summary: Extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs) are expected to be a major source of gravitational waves (GWs) for the future {\it Laser Interferometer Space Antenna} ({\it LISA}). An EMRI occurs when a compact object, driven by the emission of gravitational radiation, slowly inspirals into a massive black hole (MBH). The classical formation channel involves repeated two-body interactions within dense nuclear star clusters. However, both EMRI event rates and the expected distribution of their orbital parameters remain highly uncertain. A major source of this uncertainty is the poorly constrained ratio between gradually inspiraling EMRIs and direct plunges, which do not produce detectable GWs. While most studies of astrophysical EMRI production focus on the Schwarzschild limit, previous work examining the Kerr metric found that the spin of the central MBH can significantly affect the EMRI-to-plunge ratio. This enhancement depends sensitively on orbital inclination, yet earlier studies held inclination fixed. In this work, we develop the mathematical framework describing inclination evolution driven by two-body encounters evolving along Kerr geodesics. By implementing 3D diffusion into Monte Carlo simulations, we show that initially prograde orbits may evolve into retrograde states, thereby converting potential EMRIs into plunges or vice versa. We estimate the EMRI-to-plunge ratio and find that substantial MBH spin enhances the EMRI rate by a factor of $\sim 2.5$. Additionally, even for a non-spinning MBH, modeling the orbits as relativistic geodesics rather than Newtonian trajectories increases the number of EMRIs by a similar factor of $\sim 2.5$. The distribution of Kerr EMRI inclinations has a substantial prograde bias that may aid in identifying the subset of loss cone EMRIs within large future EMRI samples.

title: Identity Crisis: Untangling Mass-Ordering Artifacts from Compact-Object Pairing in Gravitational-Wave Populations
comment: Codes are publicly availdable on GitHub: https://github.com/SoumendraRoy/Mass_Ordering
summary: Mass distributions of binary black hole mergers inferred from gravitational-wave observations offer clues to how binaries form. These distributions conventionally label the heavier component as the primary, with mass $m_1$, and the lighter as the secondary, with mass $m_2$, such that $m_1 \geq m_2$. This ordering folds the physically labeled mass distribution along the equal-mass line, potentially reshaping the underlying population structure. In this Letter, we determine which population features can arise from mass ordering and which require genuine astrophysical structure. We show that ordering alone can produce (1) an $m_2$ distribution that declines more rapidly than the $m_1$ distribution, without intrinsic differences between the physically labeled components, and (2) an apparent concentration along equal masses, without correlations that preferentially pair black holes of equal mass. Moreover, different physically labeled populations can produce the same ordered mass distribution. Crucially, however, a preferred companion mass that remains constant as $m_1$ increases requires a characteristic mass scale already present in the physically labeled population. Applied to binary black hole mergers in the fifth Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog, our model recovers such a scale near $m_2 \simeq 50\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$. Around this scale, the merger-rate density declines much more rapidly toward higher $m_2$ than toward lower $m_2$, ruling out an equal or weaker high-$m_2$ decline at 99.45% credibility. This structure therefore requires a characteristic mass scale in at least one physically labeled component, but masses alone cannot determine which component carries it. Any formation model reproducing the observed high-mass binary black hole merger population must contain such a scale.

title: The Connection Between the Growth of Massive Black Holes and Their Dynamical Histories
comment: 12 pages, 8 figures, submitted to A&A
summary: Massive black holes (MBHs) grow through both gas accretion and mergers and it remains unclear how variations to MBH growth and dynamical histories contribute to the spread in empirical scaling relations between MBHs and their host galaxies. We examine the ex- and in-situ growth of MBHs within large-scale cosmological simulations and compare the evolution of an outlier population of under-grown MBHs to the general population. We use the Romulus25 uniform volume cosmological simulation and the RomulusC cluster zoom-in simulation to examine the growth and merger histories of MBHs. We identify central MBHs that are undergrown relative to other MBHs in similar mass galaxies and investigate their accretion, merger, and orbital histories within the simulations. The contribution of ex-situ growth increases with MBH mass, with mergers becoming increasingly important in the most massive galaxies. We find no difference between cluster and field environments in terms of the importance of ex-situ growth, which is generally very low. Under-grown MBHs have experienced fewer mergers and have had complex dynamical histories, spending significant time 'drifting' within the galaxy or 'competing' with another MBH. Other under-grown MBHs have experienced a 'late entrance' into a galaxy which until then had no central MBH. Our results demonstrate that MBH assembly is dominated by in-situ growth, which in turn is impacted by the dynamical histories of MBHs within assembling galaxies. Prolonged off-centre evolution can suppress accretion and contribute to the formation of under-grown central MBHs at $z=0$.

title: Cosmic Evolution Survey: LOFAR 144 MHz imaging of the COSMOS field
comment: 19 pages, 19 figures, 5 tables (including Appendix), submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: We present the first deep, targeted LOFAR 144 MHz source catalogue of the COSMOS field, together with the first 144 MHz source counts in this field. The data comprise 48 h of observations. Over the 2.6 sq. deg. region adopted for the catalogue analysis, the final Dutch-array image reaches a median rms sensitivity of ~100 uJy/beam at an angular resolution of 15" x 6". The resulting catalogue contains 1984 radio sources; a peak S/N >= 5 selection is adopted for the resolved/unresolved classification and source-count analysis. We characterised the catalogue using Monte Carlo source-injection and recovery simulations, including dedicated simulations of extended sources, to quantify completeness, flux-density redistribution, and morphology-dependent source-recovery effects. The catalogue reaches 90% completeness at 1.48 mJy. The resulting Euclidean-normalised differential source counts are measured down to ~0.4 mJy and show good agreement with LoTSS DR3 144 MHz source counts and with the VLA-COSMOS 3 GHz counts scaled to 144 MHz, with ~5% of catalogue sources having multiple 3 GHz counterparts within a beam-matched search region. Comparison with the VLA-COSMOS 3 GHz catalogue shows good astrometric agreement, with median offsets of Delta_RA = 0.35" (+0.03"/-0.05") and Delta_Dec = -0.83" (+0.02"/-0.03"), approximately 6% of the corresponding synthesised-beam dimensions, and no significant radial dependence across the field. The resulting catalogue provides a low-frequency view of COSMOS and a reference dataset for future deeper LOFAR observations and multiwavelength studies of this extensively characterised extragalactic field.

title: Anchoring the Chromospheric Activity$-$Rotation Relation: A Study of the Pleiades and Group X
comment: Accepted for publication in the AAS Journals
summary: We present a study of the rotation and the chromospheric H$α$ activity of low-mass stars in the $\approx$120 Myr-old Pleiades and the $\approx$400 Myr-old Group X open clusters. We combine published and new rotation periods ($P_\mathrm{rot}$) from TESS and ZTF, and use LAMOST, SDSS, and MDM spectra to measure H$α$ equivalent widths (EWs). While overall the Group X distributions of $P_\mathrm{rot}$ and EWs are as expected, detailed comparisons to the Pleiades and to the 700-Myr-old benchmark Praesepe produce some surprises. For F through mid K stars, the Group X color$-$period sequence lies between those of the Pleiades and of Praesepe, as expected. But the $P_\mathrm{rot}$ for its late K and early M dwarfs and the Praesepe slow-rotator sequence overlap, indicating that the 700 Myr-old stars have not spun down significantly despite being nearly twice as old as their Group X counterparts. In the Rossby number$-L_\mathrm{Hα}/L_\mathrm{bol}$ plane, rapid rotators in Group X are saturated, as is seen in older clusters, whereas the rapid rotators in the Pleiades show a weak but measurable dependence of $L_\mathrm{Hα}/L_\mathrm{bol}$ on rotation. This implies that the chromospheric activity$-$rotation relation attains its mature form between 120 and 400 Myr. Dividing the sample by color reveals that K, M0, and M1 dwarfs are no longer saturated by $\approx$120 Myr, M2 and M3 dwarfs become unsaturated between $\approx$400 and $\approx$700 Myr, and later M dwarfs remain largely saturated through field ages even as their saturated $L_\mathrm{Hα}/L_\mathrm{bol}$ levels decline, indicating that chromospheric evolution is not determined by rotation period alone.

title: The ePESSTO+ census of ZTF nuclear transients. I. What flares in galactic nuclei?
comment: 11 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables
summary: Transients in galactic nuclei arise from distinct processes, only some of which trace the supermassive black hole (SMBH). These include tidal disruption events (TDEs), changing-look active galactic nuclei, Bowen fluorescence flares (BFFs) and ambiguous nuclear transients, alongside supernovae that appear nuclear but are unrelated to the SMBH. Reliable classification requires spectroscopy, which will not scale to the alert volumes of the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). We aim to characterise the population of nuclear transients, to identify early observables capable of distinguishing SMBH-related flares, and TDEs in particular, from the dominant supernova background, and to assess the biases this selection introduces. We implemented a real-time filter on the Lasair broker, selecting transients from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) alert stream by nuclear coincidence with the host galaxy, with no photometric cuts, to retain SMBH-related flares in both quiescent and active hosts. The filter ran over 16 months, with candidates reported for classification through ePESSTO+ and other facilities. The filter returned 476 candidates, of which 202 were spectroscopically classified, yielding predominantly supernovae, 10 confirmed TDEs (5%) and one BFF. The mean g-r colour and the rise time separate TDEs from the supernova background. Our filter recovers 10 of the 25 TDEs classified in the same period and declination range; most misses are technical or observational rather than physical. Simple real-time filtering combined with basic photometric criteria can already isolate TDEs efficiently from nuclear transient alert streams, and high completeness is achievable. In the LSST era, where samples will be predominantly photometric, selection bias will become as important as contamination, and retaining flares in active hosts is necessary if unusual events are not to be excluded.

title: Black hole spin-mass correlation and accretion disks at birth stage of dense star clusters
comment: Talk given at the XV International Conference on New Frontiers in Physics, August 2026, Crete, Greece
summary: We review the accretion-driven channel of stellar black-hole growth and spin-up in gaseous star clusters, developed within the framework of our MSCA project "protoBH". Our detailed calculations involving semi-analytic modelling, dynamical and hydrodynamic simulations suggest that the growth and spin-up of initially low-mass stellar black holes is an integral element of the formation process of dense massive star clusters, such as the proto-globular clusters observed at high redshift. The black holes accrete residual gas, remaining from the first star formation event, and form accretion disks generated by gas angular momentum induced by the black-holes' own curved orbits. Assuming initial black hole masses below the pair-instability mass gap $\leq 55\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$, the gap gets populated with black-hole masses growing to $\sim 10^2\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$, and even reaching several hundred solar masses for sufficiently dense and massive proto-clusters. We predict a consistent spin-mass relation with low black hole spins $\lesssim 0.2$ for low black hole masses $\lesssim 20\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$, spanning all intermediate spins for higher masses and saturating to high spins $\gtrsim 0.8$ for high masses $\gtrsim 70\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$. We find evidence in favour of such an accretion-driven subpopulation of black holes in the GWTC-5.0 released by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration.

title: Delving into the depths of NGC 3783 with XRISM VI. Evidence for a failed wind based on Fe xxv absorption line variability
comment: 12 pages, 10 figures; accepted by A&A
summary: NGC 3783 exhibits a prominent Fe XXV absorption trough in the time-averaged XRISM/Resolve spectrum. To investigate its short-term variability, we present a time-resolved analysis of the Fe XXV absorption line during the continuous 10-day observation. We divided the resolved absorption profile into five fixed velocity intervals and measured their normalized equivalent widths in 19 time-resolved spectra. Three velocity intervals exhibit significant equivalent-width (EW) variability. Two velocity intervals respond differently to low- and high-flux states with less emission line contamination. The time-dependent photoionisation modelling is unable to reproduce the most significant observed EW variation ($3.5 \, σ$), possibly owing to uncertainties in the assumed initial equilibrium state, which prevent a precise density measurement. Instead, using photoionisation calculations and assuming the high-density limit, we derive approximate constraints on the ionisation parameters of the two relevant components. The low-velocity component (-320 to -680 km/s) shows a delayed inverse response, indicating a high ionisation parameter, while its relatively short lag timescale indicates a relatively high density and a distance upper limit of 0.05 pc. In contrast, the high-velocity component (-680 to -1040 km/s) manifests a positive response with a longer lag to the ionising continuum, implying a relatively low ionisation parameter. This component appears to be less dense, with an inferred distance upper limit of 0.25 pc. The low-velocity component is consistent with a failed wind, as its outflow velocity is below the local escape velocity, whereas the high-velocity component lies near the escape threshold. Together with the lower-ionisation failed wind detected in 2001, this supports a multiphase failed-wind scenario in the unobscured state of NGC~3783 over more than two decades.

title: Structure and evolution of cosmic voids within DESI DR1
comment: 17 pages, 14 figures; accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Ongoing stage IV galaxy surveys such as DESI or Euclid offer an unprecedented amount of information to study the large-scale structure of the Universe by mapping tens of millions of galaxies. Within the context of cosmic voids, already released and future catalogues will help better understand the void structure and evolution as well as the cosmological model constraints derived from their statistics. With the recent DESI Data Release 1, our aim is to obtain a new void catalogue that allows us to study the properties of cosmic voids at different redshifts, hence providing insight not only on their structure but also on their evolution. We select the DESI BGS and LRG samples for this study. Before the void-finding process, the data goes through a preprocessing pipeline tackling redshift space distortions and reconstructing the mildly non-linear velocity field. After that, the new AVISM void finder is applied to the preprocessed data, obtaining two void catalogues in different redshift bins (0.1 < z < 0.3 and 0.4 < z < 0.8), both within a 1400^3 cMpc^3 cube. We successfully recover N_BGS = 1114 and N_LRG = 216 clean voids with sizes up to ~ 65 cMpc. The void size function, 3D shape variables, density profiles, and linear bias are obtained and analysed. Both the size function and the density profiles obtained are in agreement with previous theoretical studies. The expected mass depletion in void evolution is shown by the evolution of density profiles. We obtain a roughly constant linear bias inside r < Re with mean values of 1.31 +/- 0.02 and 2.14 +/- 0.04 for BGS and LRG, respectively. Both void catalogues are publicly released.

title: EMU detection of mysterious multiple component radio-continuum emission from nearby spiral Seyfert I type galaxy 'Sand-timer' (NGC 7213)
comment: Published in the Open Journal of Astrophysics
summary: We present an Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) radio-continuum detection of the nearby spiral Seyfert I type galaxy NGC 7213 which we nickname `Sand-timer' due to its morphological appearance. We find intriguing, peculiar emission extending from the central supermassive black hole (SMBH), which we refer to as galaxy hyperbubbles and/or active galactic nucleus (AGN) jets. Finally, we find two previously undetected kiloparsec-scale features in the polarised intensity image, which appear most likely also related to the central SMBH, as restarted bipolar radio jets, though somewhat obscured in the radio-continuum total intensity image. They resemble the bow shocks often seen in Fanaroff-Riley Class II (FR-II) radio galaxies, and so we propose they most likely represent an early episode of the `Sand-timer's' AGN jet activity. An alternative scenario is that the core of NGC 7213 may be a supermassive binary black hole (SMBBH) undergoing a tidal disruption event (TDE), potentially causing the peculiar radio-continuum emission.

title: Massive black holes in the first billion years with JWST
comment: Nature Astronomy Review Article (author version)
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has unlocked uncharted territory for the study of early black holes, enabling the detection of fainter and smaller black holes at larger cosmological distances than previously possible. Compared to nearby massive black holes, they are characterised by several unexpected attributes, such as their multi-wavelength properties or their relation to their host galaxies. These observational findings challenge our understanding of the past evolution of present-day supermassive black holes, and provide novel anchor points to constrain theoretical models of black hole formation and growth. This review summarises our current understanding of the observed properties of newly discovered, active black holes in the early Universe, discusses the status of mass measurements and the relation to their hosts, as well as open questions and future prospects.

title: Low-frequency spectra and scattering of pulsars towards the Gum Nebula with the MWA
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics (A&A)
summary: Context. The Gum Nebula is a nearby ionised complex with sight-line-dependent pulsar propagation. Aims. We test whether a smooth ionised structure can explain low-frequency spectral turnovers and pulse broadening, or whether smaller-scale material is required. Methods. We analysed Murchison Widefield Array observations of six pulsars at 80--240 MHz, combining sub-band flux densities with literature data. We compared power-law, free--free absorption (FFA), and turnover-constrained broken-power-law (BPL) spectra, and modelled scattering through pulse-profile convolution. PSR J0820-4114 and the Vela pulsar were fitted jointly across frequency. Results. All six spectra depart from a single power law. FFA is favoured for PSRs J0737-3039A and J0820-4114, and BPL for J0742-2822 and J0835-4510; the other two classifications depend on assumed error floors. Conditional FFA solutions imply emission measures of $10^4$--$10^5$ pc cm$^{-6}$ for electron temperatures of $3\times10^3$--$10^4$ K, far exceeding smooth-shell expectations. PSRs J0737-3039A and J0837-4135 have scattering laws consistent with $τ_{\rm sc}\proptoν^{-4}$. We obtain $α_{\rm sc}=-3.07\pm0.11$ for J0742-2822 and $-1.59\pm0.44$ for J0820-4114 using a joint two-component model. The Vela pulsar is best described by an effective thick-screen model with $α_{\rm sc}\simeq-2.74$. Neither tested Galactic electron-density model reproduces both independent distances and low-frequency scattering uniformly. Conclusions. The results favour a structured Gum--Vela magneto-ionic environment in which neighbouring sight lines probe different absorbing and scattering material; these effects need not arise in the same plasma component.

title: CosmoForge II. An exact treatment of arbitrary linear filters in quadratic maximum-likelihood power spectrum estimation
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, prepared for submission to A&A
summary: Ground-based cosmic microwave background (CMB) experiments filter their time-ordered data to remove $1/f$ noise and ground pickup, which removes or mixes the large angular scales where primordial $B$ modes peak. A common remedy is a pseudo-$C_\ell$ estimator with harmonic $B$-purification and a transfer function measured from simulations. Another applies it after a matrix-based $E/B$ purification of the maps. We extend the quadratic maximum-likelihood (QML) estimator of CosmoForge to filtered maps, treating the filter exactly: a linear filter conjugates the estimator's ingredients without altering its structure. The same holds for the pixel-based likelihood of CosmoForge, which gives the smallest error bar achievable on the same maps. We compare all methods in a simplified setup under several map-level filters through the error bars on bandpowers and on the tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$. QML sits $2$ to $4\%$ above the pixel-likelihood bound on $σ(r)$ in every filter state. At low noise, the pure pseudo-$C_\ell$ $σ(r)$ is $1.21$ times QML's without filtering, $3.0$ times under a scan filter along stripes of constant declination, and $3.7$ times under one from a toy constant-elevation scan. The matrix-purified pseudo-$C_\ell$ $σ(r)$ is at most $1.03$ times QML's except under the constant-elevation filters, where it reaches $1.10$. These factors shrink towards unity at higher noise. The pure pseudo-$C_\ell$ gap comes from apodisation and from harmonic $E/B$ separation; pixel-space separation closes it, except under the constant-elevation filters, which attenuate modes rather than remove them and widen the gap. QML stays within a few per cent of the optimal error bars without the tuning and simulated transfer functions of the pseudo-$C_\ell$ pipelines. Thus, CosmoForge provides a robust framework for power-spectrum estimation and inference on filtered maps. (Abridged)

title: The Promise of Gravitational-Wave Astronomy
comment: Invited review for the Focus Point on Surprises from Major New Telescopes (https://link.springer.com/collections/bdijcibaac)
summary: We review the promise of upcoming gravitational-wave (GW) observations in addressing some of the important open questions in astrophysics and cosmology. A decade after the first direct detection of GWs, the field is entering a transformative phase driven by progressive detector upgrades and the anticipated advent of space-based and next-generation ground-based observatories. These instruments will not only push the distance horizon of GW observations to cosmological redshifts, but will dramatically extend the accessible frequency band, opening entirely new source classes that lie beyond the reach of current detectors. The source landscape is rich enough that surprises are likely. This review surveys our current understanding across this landscape and offers some perspective on the discoveries that upcoming GW observations are poised to deliver.

title: A 210 Megaparsec Ionized Structure at $z=6.8$ Revealed by an Astrophysics Foundation Model
comment: Updated Figures and Acknowledgments
summary: Reionization is the last major transition in the Universe that transforms the intergalactic medium (IGM) from neutral to highly ionized, yet its spatial structure remains poorly constrained. Using an astrophysics foundation model trained for James Webb Space Telescope datasets, we identify a luminous galaxy at redshift $z=7.567$ showing significant Ly$α$ transmission at $z=6.80\pm0.07$. This transmission, named ``the First Ly$α$ transmission in the Reionization Epoch at $z\sim7$" (FL$α$RE-z7), indicates a cosmological-scale ionized structure extending over $210.5^{+55.7}_{-53.5}$ comoving Megaparsecs at cosmic dawn. The hydrogen neutral fraction of the ionized structure is $x_{\rm HI}=(2.07^{+0.29}_{-0.30})\times10^{-6}$, about $10^5$ times lower than the cosmic mean at similar redshifts $(x_{\rm HI}\approx0.4)$. Cosmological simulations suggest a probability of $\approx10^{-5}$ for a random sightline to reproduce the transmission. We find no significant galaxy overdensity associated with the transmission region, in tension with canonical inside-out reionization models. FL$α$RE-z7 severely challenges existing reionization models in the standard $Λ$CDM Universe, indicating extreme spatial fluctuation in ionizing radiation or IGM temperature. Our result marks the first example of a foundation model discovering a previously unpredicted astrophysical phenomenon, demonstrating the power of deep learning methods for mining large astronomical datasets and finding unexpected new astrophysics.

title: Cosmic web Ly$α$ emission in a sample of overdense regions
comment: 17 pages, 12 Figures (+3 in appendix). Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: We present a complete and homogeneous analysis of the Ly$α$ emission properties of the cosmic web at $3 \lesssim z \lesssim 5$ as a function of the overdensity of Ly$α$ emitters (LAEs) in the MUSE Ultra Deep Field (MUDF) and the MUSE Extremely Deep Field (MXDF). We identify 41 overdensities, probing environments that are $δ\approx 2 - 10$ times denser than the field. We search for extended emission down to surface brightness (SB) levels of $3 - 5 \times 10^{-20}\ \mathrm{erg\ s^{-1}\ cm^{-2}\ arcsec^{-2}}$, revealing filamentary structures beyond the scale of the circumgalactic medium, confirming that LAEs act as signposts of the cosmic web. A trend with overdensity emerges: non-detections are mainly at $δ< 2$, a $\approx 1$ dex scatter in SB appears for $2 \lesssim δ\lesssim 3.5$, and detections reach a maximum intrinsic SB of $\approx 2 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{erg\ s^{-1}\ cm^{-2}\ arcsec^{-2}}$ for $δ\gtrsim 3.5$. Emitting regions occupy a fraction of projected area $f_s \approx 0.20 - 0.25$ inside filaments, yielding a cosmological incidence for Ly$α$ emission in the cosmic web $\ell(\mathrm{Ly}α)$ of $\approx 1.22$, which is similar to the one of partially-neutral Lyman limit systems. This analysis indicates that the emitting gas is partially ionized at moderate densities ($n_{\mathrm{H}} \approx 10^{-3} - 10^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm}^{-3}$), likely tracing the denser spines of intergalactic filaments and embedded substructures. Finally, we forecast how oriented stacking in larger samples of overdensities from shallower observations could yield an expanded view of the cosmic web before the next-generation wide-field spectroscopic instruments become operational.

title: Field-Level Baryon Acoustic Oscillation Reconstruction of the DESI DR1 Luminous Red Galaxies with Linear Field Transformer (LiFT)
comment: Submitted to JCAP. 42 pages, 15 figures, 8 tables. v2: fixed a duplicate citation and expanded references for RecIso reconstruction; minor text revisions; updated acknowledgments
summary: We present the first application of neural field-level baryon-acoustic oscillation (BAO) reconstruction to real spectroscopic survey data. We develop Linear Field Transformer (LiFT), a 3D vision transformer that takes as input the observed galaxy field, its standard reconstruction, and a set of context channels encoding local line of sight, survey coverage, and redshift, and learns to correct standard reconstruction toward the linear density field. We construct a forward-modeling pipeline to produce mock lightcones similar to the DESI Data Release 1 (DR1) luminous red galaxy (LRG) sample, and train LiFT on these. We validate LiFT on held-out simulations, as well as on additional mocks which differ in gravity solver, halo finder, HOD, cosmology, and fiber-assignment history, as well as on mocks analyzed with a distorted distance-redshift relation; ultimately, we find unbiased dilation parameters with consistently tighter constraints than standard reconstruction. Applied to the DESI DR1 LRGs, LiFT improves errors on $α_{\rm iso}$ by 13%, 24%, and 30% and on $α_{\rm AP}$ by 5%, 22%, and 30% relative to the DESI DR1 standard reconstruction analysis in the LRG1, LRG2, and LRG3 bins respectively; meanwhile, our DR1 central values remain consistent with DR1 and DR2. This equates to a factor of 1.2, 1.7 and 2.0 increase in Figure of Merit (or effective survey volume) if one were to only use standard reconstruction. Ultimately, these results establish LiFT as a validated, survey-ready tool for current and upcoming galaxy surveys.

title: Bayesian Inference of the Tip of the Red Giant Branch: I. One-Dimensional Analysis
comment: 20 pages, 15 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to the Open Journal of Astrophysics. Comments welcome
summary: The tip of the red giant branch (TRGB) is a relative distance measure that can be used, as part of a cosmic distance ladder, to infer the Hubble constant. We present a Bayesian framework for TRGB inference that incorporates selection effects and propagates per-star flux uncertainties, modelling the observed catalogue as a realisation of an inhomogeneous Poisson point process which includes the RGB and contamination from the asymptotic giant branch (AGB). We derive expressions for the predicted TRGB uncertainty in terms of the photometric noise, stellar density fainter than the tip, and the ratio of the AGB to AGB+RGB number densities, $r$. We validate these results using synthetic data from a simplified luminosity function. Applying the full model to synthetic catalogues, we find that the dependence on $r$ is the strongest of the three, and that reliable inference requires $r\lesssim0.5$; otherwise, the posterior can be multimodal, and the TRGB cannot reliably be identified. We then fit data from 11 Hubble Space Telescope fields of the calibrator galaxy NGC 4258. We find intrinsic field-to-field scatter of $τ=0.067^{+0.023}_{-0.017}$ mag (beyond the measurement noise), and a galaxy-level, extinction-corrected TRGB magnitude of $25.324 \pm 0.026$ in the F814W filter. Combining this with the maser distance modulus to NGC 4258 of $29.397 \pm 0.032$ mag, we determine the absolute magnitude of the TRGB to be $M_{\mathrm{F814W}}^{\mathrm{TRGB}} = -4.073 \pm 0.026$ (tip) $\pm 0.032$ (dist), consistent with, but brighter than, other recent analyses of the same data.

title: Little Red Dots are Direct-Collapse Black Hole-Forming Galaxies
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, accepted by ApJL
summary: "Little Red Dots" (LRDs) at $4 < z < 8$ are one of the most challenging discoveries by JWST to date because their distinctive V-shaped spectra and compact morphologies (100 - 200 pc) defy conventional astrophysical interpretation. Previous attempts to explain LRDs as compact stellar systems, heavily-cocooned black holes with differential flows, supermassive stars, or more exotic objects like 'black-hole stars' either cannot show how they formed, explain the origin of the dense shells needed for the absorption features in their spectra, or account for their observed abundances or inferred lifetimes. Here we show that LRDs are simply direct-collapse black hole galaxies in which the BH is still shrouded by the massive disk that created it. Our cosmological simulations yield spectra that are good matches to those of LRDs because high densities at the center of the disk trap X-rays from the BH and produce the observed Balmer absorption features while allowing UV, optical and reprocessed IR flux to partly escape. The host galaxy forms a dense 10$^8$ M$_{\odot}$ cluster of stars with a radius of 150 pc next to the BH, consistent with observations of LRDs. Our models reproduce a wide variety of LRD spectra from typical objects like RUBIES-EGS-42046 at $z = 5.28$ to those with the strongest Balmer breaks such as MoM-BH$^*$-1 at $z = 7.76$ and those at the highest redshifts like CAPERS-LRD-z9 at $z = 9.29$.

title: Color-Kinematics Duality and the Double Copy in Curved Spacetimes
comment: 191 pages plus appendices and references, invited review article for Physics Reports; v2 fixed typos, updated references, and improved some discussions; v3 updated references
summary: The double copy relates gravitational data to gauge-theory data, most sharply through color-kinematics duality for flat-space scattering amplitudes. This review surveys the extent to which this idea can be formulated beyond asymptotically flat backgrounds. After recalling the flat-space ingredients needed for comparison, we describe curved-space constructions for boundary correlators and scattering observables in AdS, dS, and other non-trivial backgrounds. We then review classical and field-level maps, including Kerr--Schild, Weyl, Cotton, twistor, and convolutional double copies. A separate part is devoted to self-dual sectors. Throughout, we emphasize both the common structures that survive from flat space and the obstructions introduced by curvature.

title: Scalar-induced gravitational waves from a box-shaped curvature power spectrum
comment: 34 pages, 5 figures, JCAP accepted
summary: We compute the stochastic background of gravitational waves (GWs) produced at second order in cosmological perturbation theory by a primordial curvature power spectrum that is flat in $\ln k$ over a finite band $[k_-,k_+]=[k_*e^{-Δ},k_*e^{+Δ}]$ and vanishes elsewhere. This logarithmic box interpolates between a monochromatic spectrum as $Δ\to0$ and a locally scale-invariant plateau as $Δ\to\infty$, and its sharp boundaries make the geometry of the source convolution unusually transparent. Working in the radiation era, we reduce the convolution to a compact integral over the overlap between the momentum triangle and the box, and evaluate it analytically in two regimes. For a narrow box we show that, to leading order in the width, the spectrum equals the Dirac-spectrum result multiplied by a purely geometric overlap factor $Φ_{\rm box}(κ,Δ)$; this factor turns the infrared slope from $k^{3}\ln^{2}k$ into $k^{2}\ln^{2}k$ at a break $k_b=2k_*\sinhΔ$. For a broad box we separate the lower edge, the scale-invariant interior, and the upper edge, derive the leading behaviour in each (an infrared $k^{3}\ln^{2}k$ rise, a scale-invariant plateau, and a quartic cut-off at the hard endpoint $k=2k_+$), and combine them into a single uniform formula cast as a product of two universal, $Δ$-independent edge functions. We also provide an integral-free closed-form surrogate for these edge functions for use in parameter scans.

title: Boundary-supported radial layering in Hoag-like ring galaxies
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures; submitted to MNRAS Letters
summary: Clean Hoag-like ring galaxies are often characterized by an old compact central component, a depleted gap, and a detached outer ring. We identify a boundary-supported radial-layering mechanism in a shell-deformed Kepler control model. A compact inner boundary supplies the core state, while a localized effective shell deformation, interpreted as the reduced imprint of externally supplied material settled near a finite circularization radius, needs to create only an internal maximum and a subsequent outer minimum. These act as the gap barrier and ring-supporting well. The onset of this structure is organized by a saddle-node threshold of the critical-point equation. In a 10^4-point Monte Carlo scan, shell-localized boundary-supported candidates occupy finite parameter volume under the adopted priors, and none of the localized candidates contains an ordered interior minimum--maximum--minimum subsequence. The same branch gives a scale-free gap-to-ring interval overlapping representative ratios for Hoag's Object, UGC 4599, and PGC 1000714, but not for the environmentally processed comparison object JO171.

title: The Three Hundred project: cosmic web identification from 2D gas and Compton-$y$ maps of galaxy clusters outskirts
comment: 12 pages, 9 figures. Published in A&A on 12/10/2026. Reproduced with permission from Astronomy & Astrophysics, copyright ESO
summary: Galaxy clusters are located at the nodes of the filamentary network known as the cosmic web. A more comprehensive understanding of galaxy clusters can be achieved by considering their environment, in particular, the filamentary structures to which they are connected. In this work, we aim to assess the reliability of the cosmic web reconstruction from mock observational data. In particular, we aim to quantify the effects of the 2D projection relative to the underlying 3D network and the impact of using the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (SZ) effect as a tracer of the cosmic web. We reconstruct the filamentary networks in the outskirts of The Three Hundred simulated clusters with the filament finder DisPerSE. First, we extract the networks from the 2D gas distribution and evaluate their purity and completeness with respect to the 3D networks projected along the line of sight. We also compute the distances between the corresponding skeletons. Moreover, we identify filaments from simulated Compton-$y$ maps of the clusters at redshift $z=0$, and we compare them with the 2D gas network. The skeletons extracted from 2D maps provide good representations of the underlying 3D ones, both in terms of critical points and filaments. We find a median distance between the spines of the 2D and projected 3D networks of approximately $0.22 \, h^{-1}$ Mpc, although the connectivity derived from the 2D networks is slightly underestimated. We observe a good spatial agreement between the gas and SZ networks, with a median distance of $\approx 0.24 \, h^{-1}$ Mpc. Finally, we show that gas outside galaxy clusters is preferentially located in filamentary structures, which contribute $\sim 80\%$ of the integrated Compton-$Y$ parameter of clusters' outskirts.

title: The DESIRED strong-line calibrations: I. New empirical metallicity relations for the local and high-redshift universe
comment: 50 pages, 22 figures, MNRAS accepted
summary: We present the most comprehensive set of empirical optical strong-line metallicity calibrations to date, based on the DEep Spectra of Ionised REgions Database (DESIRED), the largest compilation of HII regions and galaxies with direct electron-temperature determinations. We construct a high-quality calibration sample of 2392 spectra: 1029 extragalactic HII regions, 1296 local star-forming galaxies, and 67 high-redshift ($z > 2$) galaxies, drawn from 201 independent literature references, spanning $12+\log({\rm O/H}) \in [6.79, 9.07]$. Physical conditions and chemical abundances are derived homogeneously using up-to-date atomic data. We derive 27 strong-line calibrations covering oxygen-, nitrogen-, sulphur-, argon-, and neon-based line ratios, including 4 previously uncalibrated diagnostics, with reported validity ranges and intrinsic dispersions (typically $\sim0.15-0.35$~dex). For the first time in a systematic calibration framework, all relations are presented for both the homogeneous temperature case ($t^2 = 0$) and a scenario including temperature inhomogeneities ($t^2 > 0$), thereby reconciling abundances from recombination lines (RLs) and collisionally excited lines (CELs) and directly tackling the abundance discrepancy problem. A comparison with previous calibrations shows that the DESIRED relations span the broadest validity intervals while remaining anchored to the empirical data. Comparisons with $z>2$ galaxies show that several DESIRED calibrations remain consistent with independent high-redshift relations within their intrinsic scatter, whereas others display systematic offsets associated with elevated N/O or harder ionising conditions. Thus, DESIRED calibrations can provide reliable metallicity estimates at high redshift for a subset of diagnostics, while highlighting the need to account for diagnostic-specific redshift evolution.

title: Witnessing the Earliest Phases of Galactic Wind Formation in Superluminous Supernova Hosts: Implications for Star-formation-driven Outflows in Low- and High-redshift Galaxies
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables; accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Direct observational constraints on the earliest phases of galactic outflows remain scarce. We present Very Large Telescope/X-shooter spectroscopy of seven Type I superluminous supernova (SLSN-I) host galaxies at $z = 0.15 - 0.51$, exploiting the bright SLSN continua as down-the-barrel probes of the host interstellar medium. Five of the seven hosts exhibit narrow, blueshifted MgII $λλ$2796,2803 absorption, indicative of the presence of low-ionized outflows. Voigt modeling of the MgII absorption yields bulk outflow velocities of $45-99 {\rm ~km~s^{-1}}$ and terminal velocities of $v_{\rm max} \simeq 103-164 {\rm ~km~s^{-1}}$ the latter being below the ones reported for more evolved galaxies of similarly low mass and star formation rate. Given the expected short lifetimes of massive SLSN progenitors, we argue that these outflows are most naturally explained as originating during the preceding stellar-wind-dominated phase. We derive wind masses of $M_{\rm wind} \simeq 10^{4}-10^{5} M_{\odot}$, mass outflow rates comparable to or lower than the star formation rates, and kinetic energies of $10^{51}-10^{52}$ erg. These energies represent only a modest fraction ($\simeq 10\%$) of the mechanical energy expected from stellar winds during the first few Myr, demonstrating that the observed outflows can be powered entirely by pre-supernova feedback. Together with their low terminal velocities, these results support a scenario in which stellar winds and radiation pressure dominate the early acceleration of cold outflows, before core-collapse supernovae become dynamically important. Our work provides one of the first empirical constraints on early feedback phases relevant for high-redshift galaxies and for time-dependent implementations of stellar feedback in galaxy formation simulations.

title: Learning to See Sharper: A Physics-Informed Artificial Intelligence Framework for Super-Resolving Galaxy Spectra
comment: 18 Pages, 11 Figures, Submitted to ApJ
summary: The information recoverable from galaxy spectra depends fundamentally on spectral resolution, yet assembling large samples at high resolution remains observationally expensive. We present a deep-learning framework for spectral super-resolution that enhances low-resolution galaxy spectra by a factor of $\sim$10 in resolving power ($R\sim100$ to $R\sim1000$). The model is trained on 2,858 paired JWST/NIRSpec observations from the JADES program, where low-resolution prism spectra are matched with medium-resolution grating spectra (G140M, G235M, G395M) combined into a unified reference covering $1.0-5.3μ\mathrm{m}$. Our three-stage architecture performs an initial super-resolution, infers the redshift from the coarse reconstruction, and then applies a physics-informed residual refinement that uses attention across emission-line tokens to learn inter-line relationships and predict parametric line profiles, alongside a convolutional branch for continuum corrections. Evaluated on a 20% held-out sample, the model achieves noise-limited residuals over most of the spectral range and improves the signal-to-noise ratio of key diagnostic lines including [OII], H$β$, [OIII], and H$α$. The super-resolved spectra separate features that are entirely unresolved at prism resolution, such as the [OIII] $λ\lambda4959,5007$ doublet and H$β$, in exchange for a modest retrieval of line fluxes. As a proof of concept using JWST data, this approach is readily extensible to the low-resolution grism spectroscopy that will be delivered by Euclid and the Roman Space Telescope, potentially enabling population-level diagnostics across millions of galaxy spectra that would otherwise be inaccessible at low-resolution.

title: Looking for non-gaussianity in Pulsar Timing Arrays through the four point correlator
summary: Pulsar Timing Arrays have recently reported strong evidence for a stochastic gravitational wave background. In standard analyses, it is modeled through pulsar-dependent Fourier coefficients assumed to follow gaussian statistics, so that the signal is fully characterized by its two-point function. However, if the background arises from a finite population of inspiralling supermassive black hole binaries, non-gaussian features may emerge, making the determination of higher-order correlators essential. In this work, we compute the complete four-point correlator of the stochastic gravitational wave background Fourier coefficients for four arbitrary pulsar positions, identifying it as the leading probe of non-gaussianity. The result separates into a gaussian contribution, proportional to the square of the two-point function, and a genuinely non-gaussian connected component, whose non-trivial angular dependence generalizes the Hellings and Downs correlation to four pulsars. This angular structure depends only on averages of products of antenna pattern functions, and is therefore expected to be independent of the specific physical origin of the background. We further propose to incorporate the four-point correlator into the parameter-estimation pipeline by deriving a marginalized likelihood that perturbatively accounts for non-gaussian effects. Our results provide the theoretical framework to search for non-gaussian features in pulsar timing array data, opening the way to a more complete characterization of gravitational-wave backgrounds.

title: Symmetries of cosmological perturbations: The residual low-multipole ambiguity
comment: 34 pages without appendices (45 pages in total), matches published version in JCAP
summary: In cosmology, long-wavelength modes are related to large-gauge transformations (LGT), i.e. changes of coordinates that modify the physical geometry of the cosmological patch. These LGTs stand as bona-fide symmetries of cosmological perturbation theory with various applications, from consistency relations constraining cosmological correlators to non-linear conservation laws in the separate-universe approach. In this work, we revisit LGTs and derive two new results. First, we show that the global symmetries already identified in the literature can be extended to local infinite-dimensional symmetries. The associated generators depend on arbitrary functions of time, and generate low-multipole modes that modify the mean curvature energy and the angular momentum of the patch, demonstrating their physical nature. We propose to interpret these low-multipole soft modes as a new cosmological-frame ambiguity that needs to be fixed prior to evaluating cosmological observables. Second, we demonstrate that the adiabatic cosmological perturbations generated by LGTs deform but preserve all the explicit and hidden Killing symmetries of the background geometry. As such, long-wavelength modes stand as a concrete example of algebraically-special cosmological perturbations of Petrov-type O, and inherit the conformal group as isometries and a set of four deformed Killing-Yano tensors and their associated Killing tensors. This opens the possibility to study their effect on cosmological observables in a fully analytic manner.

title: Evidence of galaxy cluster rotation and intrahalo gas motions in the cosmic microwave background
