comment: Updated to match published version in PRL
summary: We report the first robust evidence for the rotational kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (rkSZ) effect: the dipolar signal produced by the Thomson scattering of cosmic microwave background (CMB) photons off intracluster gas in dynamically active systems (including rotations and mergers). By combining CMB intensity and polarization measurements from the \emph{Planck} satellite with spectroscopic member-galaxy redshifts from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey in a sample of 25 X-ray cross-matched, low-redshift ($0.02< z< 0.09)$, massive ($10^{13.9}\lesssim M_{\rm 500c}/M_\odot \lesssim 10^{14.6}$) galaxy clusters, we detect a dipolar rkSZ signature aligned with the estimated angular momentum of each cluster, ruling out a chance fluctuation at 99.98\% confidence (3.6$σ$). The significance of this measurement is enhanced by several new methodological improvements for isolating the rkSZ signal from primary CMB fluctuations and noise. The amplitude and shape of the signal are qualitatively consistent with predictions from state-of-the-art hydrodynamical simulations. These results establish a new tool with which to probe the dynamical state of galaxy clusters using CMB data.

title: Collective Properties of Gravitational Perturbations in Thermal Environments on a Dynamical Background
comment: 31 pages, 3 figures. Substantially revised and expanded from the previous letter version into a regular article
summary: A thermal plasma dresses soft gauge fields, turning them into collective modes with a plasmon gap and Landau damping. In this paper, we ask whether a thermal radiation plasma does the same to gravitational perturbations. For gravity, the thermal soft scale coincides with the Hubble rate. Any such gap therefore lies at the horizon scale, where the expansion of the background cannot be neglected. We model radiation by a conformal scalar and compute its linear response to metric perturbations directly on a flat FLRW background. We test this response against the diffeomorphism Ward identities. The adiabatic dispersion relation yields a gapped collective mode with $ω_p^2 = 8\mathcal{H}^2/5$, where $\mathcal{H}$ is the conformal Hubble rate. The imaginary part of its frequency, however, is dominated by the background expansion and does not represent Landau damping. In the radiation background, the tensor modes obey a real-time integro-differential equation that reproduces Weinberg's damping of gravitational waves. The initial-time boundary of the retarded response keeps superhorizon modes frozen until horizon reentry despite the gap. The superhorizon growth found in earlier analyses arises from discarding the memory of the retarded response and from a local-equilibrium state prescription that violates the Ward identities. More generally, the Ward identities forbid any local state response beyond the collisionless kernel.

title: Cosmic evolution of the [CII]-to-dense neutral gas relation
summary: The [CII] 158 $μ$m line is widely used to trace star formation and the gas contents of high-redshift galaxies. However, it remains unclear under which physical conditions it reliably traces the molecular reservoir, and whether a unique conversion factor $α_{\rm [CII]}$ can be applied across cosmic time. We investigated the evolution of the relation between the [CII] luminosity and dense neutral gas mass from $z\simeq10$ to $z\simeq0.2$ using the Vintergatan simulation, a high-resolution cosmological zoom-in of a Milky Way-like galaxy. We post-processed the snapshots with the SKIRT radiative transfer code to generate synthetic [CII] data cubes. We measured global and spatially resolved (100 pc) relations between [CII] luminosity ($L_{\rm [CII]}$), star formation rate (SFR), and dense neutral gas mass ($M_{\rm DN}$). We followed the redshift evolution of the [CII]-to-molecular gas conversion factor $α_{\rm [CII]}$, and link these trends to the evolution of the interstellar medium (ISM) phases. The global $L_{\rm [CII]}$-$M_{\rm DN}$ and $L_{\rm [CII]}$-SFR relations evolve from a steep, [CII]-deficient regime at very low metallicity to an almost linear behaviour, similar to calibrations at $z\approx2$, once the ISM reaches $Z \gtrsim 0.05$-$0.1\,Z_\odot$ at $z\lesssim5$. Over this evolution, $α_{\rm [CII]}$ spans nearly three orders of magnitude, from $\gtrsim 10^4$ down to $\approx10 \,\rm{M_\odot\,L_\odot^{-1}}$, even though the [CII] emission remains spatially correlated with the dense neutral gas. A unique, redshift-independent $α_{\rm [CII]}$ therefore cannot recover dense neutral gas masses across the regimes we explored. [CII] remains a viable tracer of dense neutral gas at very high redshifts, but only when used with conversion factors that explicitly account for metallicity, ISM phase mix, and merger events.

title: How JWST is Revolutionizing Our View of Early Galaxy Formation
comment: 41 pages, 25 figures, 1 table, invited review, accepted for publication in Contemporary Physics
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has been revolutionizing our understanding of early galaxy formation over its first four years of science operations. With un- precedented sensitivity, spatial resolution, and wavelength coverage from the near- to mid-infrared, JWST has enabled astronomers to identify hundreds of star-forming galaxies at redshifts z>~8 (within ~650 million years of the Big Bang) through strong spectral breaks and characterize these galaxies through sensitive spectroscopy. These capabilities have provided new insights into the stellar populations, neutral gas, nebular continuum emission, chemical enrichment, dust content, and ionization conditions of galaxies during cosmic dawn, revealing more numerous and brighter systems than anticipated from pre-JWST models. We discuss the implications of these discoveries for reionization, the buildup of stellar mass and metals, and the evolution of galaxy populations and luminosity functions. JWST is also revealing a new physical picture of early galaxies, characterized by compact, clumpy star formation, high gas fractions, and intense radiation fields. Despite much progress, many open questions remain, including the efficiency, intermittency, and stellar initial mass function (IMF) of early star formation, conditions in the interstellar medium (ISM), masses, and structure of the earliest galaxies, and the topology of reionization. Resolving these open questions will require lensing magnification, sensitive spectroscopy to > 5 micron, including with the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA), exploration to higher redshifts, and larger, more complete samples, helping to clarify how the first galaxies formed and evolved.

title: Radio ghosts: Radio polarimetry study of newly discovered cluster minihalo candidates or radio tailed galaxies
comment: 14 pages, 11 figures
summary: Extended diffuse radio emission in the central regions of galaxy clusters is commonly associated with non-thermal processes in the intracluster medium (ICM), but its origin and the mechanisms responsible for sustaining it remain uncertain. We present the discovery and multi-wavelength analysis of two diffuse radio sources, MKTJ0355-4237 and MKTJ0355-4230, to assess their nature and investigate their radio spectral and magnetic field properties through radio polarimetric analysis. We use deep MeerKAT L-band (1.28 GHz) observations to perform spectral analysis of the diffuse emission and study its polarisation properties via rotation measure synthesis. These are complemented by eROSITA X-ray data and DESI photometric redshift catalogues to characterise the host cluster environments. MKTJ0355-4237 is confirmed as cluster-scale minihalo with extent of $\sim 400$ kpc, while the other diffuse source MKTJ0355-4230 remain uncertain and could be either associated with a radio minihalo or radio tailed galaxy. Both show steep spectra ($α\approx -0.7$ to $-0.8$) that steepen toward the outskirts ($α\lesssim -2.5$), consistent with spatial variations in electron ageing and re-acceleration. Polarised emission is detected in both systems, with fractional polarisation $\sim1\,\%$ in the centres and increasing in the outer regions of MKTJ0355-4237. MKTJ0355-4230 is associated with a previously uncatalogued cluster and shows an X-ray morphology offset from the brightest cluster galaxy, indicative of dynamical activity. MKTJ0355-4237 exhibits a sharply bounded internal radio deficit without a corresponding X-ray counterpart, within current sensitivity limits. The spectral steepening supports turbulent re-acceleration as the origin of the diffuse emission.

title: Shear-kSZ: A New Estimator for the Matter-Electron Power Spectrum from kSZ Tomography and Weak Lensing
comment: 30 pages, 14 figures
summary: We propose a new estimator of the electron--matter power spectrum, $P_{me}(k)$, which correlates the kinematic Sunyaev--Zel'dovich (kSZ) temperature with the product of the line-of-sight velocity field and the weak-lensing convergence. Like the stacked kSZ estimator, it factorizes into a calibratable velocity kernel times $P_{me}(k)$, but it probes the full matter distribution rather than the gas around a biased tracer. It therefore measures the baryonic suppression of the matter power spectrum, $S(k)$, one of the dominant astrophysical systematics for Stage-IV cosmic shear. We derive an analytic expression for the estimator, validate it against simulations at the per-cent level, and show that its parity structure cancels cosmic microwave background (CMB) foregrounds. We forecast the detectability with a realistic pipeline: velocities reconstructed from the simulated tracers, with and without photometric-redshift errors; the kSZ signal of all the ionized gas along the line of sight; a CMB map with Simons Observatory (SO) noise; and LSST source samples free of intrinsic alignments. A DESI-like spectroscopic sample at $0.5<z<1$ over the $20\%$ of the sky that DESI, LSST and SO share gives a $4$--$7σ$ detection. Photometric redshifts cost only $5$--$10\%$ of the significance, so LSST can supply its own velocity tracers over its full overlap with SO: with tracers at $0.1<z<1.3$ and five source samples we find $10σ$ in an end-to-end simulation, and $13σ$ with Advanced SO (16$σ$ if extending to $z < 1.5$). This corresponds to a few-per-cent measurement of $S(k)$ at $k\simeq1$--$4\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$, the scales that matter most for cosmic shear.

title: Transients and Stellar Activity as Revealed by Ultraviolet Diagnostic Tracers
comment: 68 pages, incl. 7 figures. Space Science Reviews, in press; joint review paper resulting from the April 2025 ISSI-BJ Workshop on Space-based Stellar Astrophysics in the Ultraviolet
summary: Ultraviolet (UV) observations offer unique insights into transient and variable astrophysical phenomena, from the Sun and nearby stars to supernovae and star-forming galaxies. Here, we summarise and review the diagnostic power of the UV spectrum for probing the physical conditions, dynamics and energetics of these events. We trace the historical development of UV astronomy from early satellite missions to the current landscape shaped by the Hubble Space Telescope, the GALaxy Evolution eXplorer, the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and AstroSat/UVIT. Particular emphasis is placed on resonance lines such as Mg II $h$ and $k$, C II, Si IV, C IV and N V, which probe the (solar and) stellar chromosphere and transition region, revealing magnetic heating, shocks and mass loss across stellar types. We examine UV diagnostics of stellar flares, pre-main-sequence activity and rotation--activity correlations, linking them to exoplanetary irradiation and habitability. We then explore the UV view of supernova shock breakout and early-time emission, as well as the far-UV mapping of young stellar populations and hierarchical star formation in the Magellanic Clouds. Together, these aspects illustrate how the UV connects small-scale plasma processes to galactic-scale star formation. Despite remarkable progress, UV transient astronomy remains limited by instrument availability and cadence. Forthcoming missions promise to transform this field by capturing the rapid, luminous phenomena that define the dynamic Universe.

title: The Atacama Cosmology Telescope: DR6 Constraints on Isotropic Time-Dependent Cosmic Birefringence from Axion-like Particles
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures, to be submitted to PRD
summary: Axion-like particles (ALPs) with sufficiently low masses are dark matter candidates because they could account for much or all of the observed dark matter energy density and help explain observations of galactic substructure. Such pseudoscalar fields could couple to photons, causing a time-dependent rotation of the polarization of the light with an oscillation frequency equal to the ALP mass. We use measurements of the polarization of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) by the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) between 2017 and 2022 to search for this effect using an EB power spectrum estimator. By probing oscillation periods from days to years, the data constrain the coupling between ALPs and photons for ALP masses between $2.5\times 10^{-23}$ eV and $4.8\times 10^{-20}$ eV. We find no evidence for such a signal and set a 95% upper bound on the axion-photon coupling constant, $g_{ϕγ} < 1.1\times10^{-11}\left({m_ϕ}/{10^{-21}\,\mathrm{eV}}\right)\,\mathrm{GeV}^{-1} .$ This limit assumes that ALPs make up all of the dark matter and that the ALP field amplitude is stochastically distributed, which leads to more conservative bounds than the deterministic-field assumption used in some previous CMB polarization analyses. Among searches for ALP-photon coupling using CMB polarization, we set the strongest bounds to date under the stochastic-field assumption. This work develops a methodology to analyze over 10,000 time-sliced "depth-1" polarization maps from ACT, a data product that will be standard for time-domain astrophysics with the Simons Observatory, enabling searches with a higher sensitivity and observing span.

title: The connection between massive galaxies and their dark matter haloes from $z=0.25$ to $z \sim 4$ from the combined COSMOS, XMM-LSS and ECDF-S fields
comment: 28 pages, 18 figures, 3 tables, Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Understanding how galaxies populate and grow within dark matter haloes is essential for linking the observed evolution of galaxies to the hierarchical growth of structure. We present a galaxy clustering analysis using optical and near-infrared data from the UltraVISTA and VIDEO surveys covering $9.3$ deg$^2$ across the COSMOS, XMM-LSS and ECDF-S fields, $\sim 5\times$ larger than previous comparable studies, providing sufficient volume to determine the halo occupation of the most massive galaxies to $z\sim 4$. We measure the angular two-point correlation function for stellar-mass-selected galaxies over $0.25<z<4$ and by combining the three fields, we reduce the cosmic variance by a factor of $\sim2$ compared to the individual fields. The stellar-to-halo mass ratio peaks at a halo mass of $M_{h}\approx10^{12} {\rm M}_{\odot}$ and is a maximum at $z\sim 1$. For the most massive galaxies, the peak halo mass ($M_{h}^{\rm peak}$) increases from $z=1\rightarrow 0$, while the peak stellar mass in such haloes remains approximately constant, indicating that at $z<1$ massive galaxy formation becomes less efficient. We also find a steady increase in the satellite fraction since $z\sim 1$, from which we infer that massive halos continue to grow hierarchically while their central galaxies experience suppressed stellar-mass growth. We suggest this is due to the central massive galaxies having their growth controlled by feedback from active galactic nuclei feedback, likely from low-power stochastic radio emission.

title: MUSE-DARK IV. Comparing Dark Matter Densities to Star Formation Histories in 375 intermediate-z galaxies
comment: Submitted to A&A, comments are welcome
summary: (Abridged) Baryonic feedback is expected to transform cuspy dark-matter (DM) haloes into cores, but direct observational links between inner DM slopes and galaxy star-formation histories (SFHs) remain limited. We investigate and quantify the connection between halo inner slopes and baryonic assembly histories in a large sample of intermediate-z galaxies. We analyse 375 galaxies at 0.1<z<1.43 spanning 7<log(Mstar/Msun)<11.2 using 3D forward modelling of MUSE kinematics and disk-halo decompositions with mass-dependent (DC14-based) and generalised Navarro-Frenk-White (gNFW) halo profiles. Stellar population parameters are inferred from multi-band Spectral Energy Distribution fitting of UV-to-MIR photometry using a non-parametric SFH model. Bayesian model comparison shows that the DC14-based halo density profiles are statistically preferred over gNFW for a substantial fraction of the sample. The inferred inner slopes from gNFW fits nevertheless follow the DC14 expectation and reproduce the expected dependence on the stellar-to-halo mass ratio, despite this not being explicitly imposed. Partial correlation coefficient and random forest regression analyses consistently identify stellar mass (or, equivalently, the stellar-to-halo mass ratio) as the primary driver of the inner density slope, a result that holds robustly even when the analysis is restricted to the gNFW fits. In contrast, SFH-related quantities (e.g. formation time and 'burstiness' indicators) exhibit no independent predictive power on the DM halo inner slope once the dependence on stellar mass is accounted for. Cored systems preferentially occupy lower-mass, more bursty bins with later assembly times, whereas cuspy systems are associated with higher stellar masses, lower star formation activity, and earlier assembly epochs, in agreement with theoretical expectations of stellar-feedback-induced cores.

title: Phase Separation of HI in the Draco Nebula: CNM formation Triggered by Colliding WNM Flows
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan (PASJ)
summary: We investigate the thermal phase structures and kinematics of atomic hydrogen (H I) gas in the Draco nebula to clarify how infalling H I evolves toward cold atomic and molecular clouds. Using the DHIGLS H I 21 cm data, we apply the Regularized Optimization for Hyper-Spectral Analysis (ROHSA) algorithm to decompose the emission into spatially coherent Gaussian components, and classify them as warm neutral medium (WNM), lukewarm neutral medium (LNM), and cold neutral medium (CNM). We identify two kinematically distinct WNM components: WNM1 near $-3$ km s$^{-1}$ and WNM2 near $-30$ km s$^{-1}$. The LNM forms a broad velocity bridge between two WNMs, whereas the CNM is concentrated within a narrower intermediate velocity range. CO emission is also confined to this interval and is associated with CNM-rich regions. The H I mass fractions are $\sim 41\%$, $\sim 23\%$, $\sim 17\%$, and $\sim 19\%$ for WNM1, WNM2, LNM, and CNM, respectively, with the LNM and CNM together accounting for $\sim 36\%$ of the total H I mass. No comparably independent WNM component is recovered at intermediate velocities, although a weak broad component may remain unresolved. The observed phase structures are consistent with a dynamically compressed multiphase interaction layer in which compression increases the gas density, shortens the radiative cooling time, and drives the evolution from WNM through thermally unstable gas toward the CNM. The present interaction may both create new CNM, and further compress or grow pre-existing dense structures. Our results provide the missing link between previous evidence for dynamical interaction and molecular cloud formation in Draco, and identify CNM formation as a key step in transforming gas accreting toward the Galactic disk into cold atomic and molecular clouds.

title: Sulphur-bearing molecule survey towards prestellar and starless cores in the Perseus molecular cloud
summary: Sulphur is drastically depleted from the gas phase in dense starless and prestellar cores, creating the long-standing "missing sulphur problem". Observations of sulphur-bearing molecules are crucial to understanding sulphur chemistry, core-environment relationships, and the physical evolution of star-forming regions. We present a survey of four sulphur-bearing molecules, HCS+, OCS, H2CS, and SO, towards 15 starless and prestellar cores in the Perseus molecular cloud using the Yebes 40m telescope. The HCS+ 1-0, OCS 3-2 and 4-3, H2CS 1_{0,1}-0_{0,0}, and SO 3_2-2_2 transitions were observed, fitted with Gaussian profiles, and column densities were calculated assuming local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE). We also compare these with observations of CS, CCS, and CCCS from a previous study. HCS+, OCS, H2CS, and SO are detected in 100%, 93%, 100%, and 73% of the sample, respectively. Derived column densities are (2.2-17.0)x10^11 cm^-2 for HCS+, (1.9-25.0)x10^12 cm^-2 for OCS, (1.0-15.0)x10^12 cm^-2 for H2CS, and (0.3-17.0)x10^13 cm^-2 for SO, spanning over an order of magnitude. HCS+ and SO abundances strongly correlate (inversely and directly, respectively) with core volume density, reinforcing their early- and late-type status. Correlations indicate a differentiation between carbon and oxygen chemistry for sulphur-bearing molecules, with CS showing the strongest correlations as expected. Cores in protostellar outflow paths do not show consistently higher abundances. The chemical age (SO/CS) correlates with physical age (volume density), except for Per752, an outlier likely linked to an enhanced cosmic ray ionization rate. These results provide a robust observational baseline constraining chemical models of sulphur chemistry in early star formation.

title: Gravitational Properties of the Monopole Bag
comment: 47 pages, 8 figures (version accepted by JHEP, some discussions added, no change to figures)
summary: Axionic cosmologies constitute a class of models with phenomenologically rich symmetry breaking in the early universe. In the case where monopoles are present in such a background, the axion profile may be deformed; it is possible to construct a ``monopole bag" state composed of a central monopole within a closed axion domain wall. We consider the gravitational properties of this composite defect, and propose that there exist both a horizonless and a black hole-like static solution for different input parameters. For the latter case, we present our results as a first step towards a new construction of a dyonic regular black hole, given the monopole bag's potential ability to evade the usual singular gravitational collapse and retain a non-trivial axionic profile by the exotic electromagnetic properties of an axionic Chern-Simons term.

title: Implications of Cosmic Birefringence for Multi-Field ALP Dark Matter
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures
summary: Cosmic birefringence, characterized by the observed rotation of the polarization plane of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation, serves as a critical probe for testing theories beyond the standard cosmological scenario. As a major component of the universe, dark matter plays a pivotal role in cosmic evolution, particularly in the formation of large-scale structures. However, its fundamental nature remains elusive. Axion-like particles (ALPs), as promising dark matter candidates, possess unique advantages in naturally explaining such phenomena. Previous studies on the implications of cosmic birefringence for these ultralight ALP fields have focused on single-field models with conventional potentials. These models face exclusion due to the washout effect - a suppression of the CMB polarization power spectrum induced by oscillatory dynamics of the scalar field within the mass range of less than $10^{-23}$ eV. To address this limitation, we develop a more general theoretical framework incorporating two ALP fields, providing analytical approximations and numerical calculations. Our findings reveal that the superposition of two ALP fields with distinct masses can relax the constraints imposed by the washout effect and reconcile with observations.

title: Are Broad Mg II Galaxies Fading AGN?
comment: ApJ accepted. 32 pages, 23 figures. In the Appendix, we present the results of a PyQSOFit investigation where we vary the number of Monte Carlo samples for error estimation to assess the impact on measurement precision, measurement accuracy, and computing time. The results can serve as a guide for planning the error analysis when decomposing hundreds to thousands of spectra with PyQSOFit
summary: We analyzed a sample of 494 galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) I-IV that have unusual properties. They display broadened Mg II $λ$2798 line emission, as would be expected of Type 1 active galactic nuclei (AGN). However, they have weak or absent broad Balmer lines though broadened Balmer lines often accompany broadened ultraviolet lines in Type 1 AGN spectra. We performed a spectral decomposition of these "broad Mg II galaxies'' to assess whether they can be considered fading AGN. The Balmer lines are more responsive to changes in the AGN continuum than the Mg II line. As the AGN power source fades, broad H$β$ and then H$α$ will weaken and eventually disappear, leaving broad Mg II as a signpost of a more active past. In support of this interpretation, we found that broad Mg II galaxies have weaker AGN luminosities and lower accretion rates (parameterized by the Eddington ratio) than typical Type 1 quasars from SDSS. The Eddington ratio of broad Mg II galaxies are similar to dim-state changing-look AGN, with an average value $\lesssim$1\%, which is the threshold at which the inner region of a geometrically thin accretion disk is thought to evaporate and be replaced by a geometrically thick radiatively inefficient accretion flow in stellar-mass black holes. Broad Mg II galaxies may represent the penultimate stage in a changing-look AGN sequence prior to the complete disappearance of all broad lines.

title: jax-SNANA: A GPU-accelerated Supernova Framework for the SBI Era
comment: Submitted
summary: We present jax-SNANA, a JAX reimplementation of the supernova analysis framework SNANA. jax-SNANA enables GPU-accelerated transient simulations and light curve fitting, supernova standardisation and cosmological inference. Running in single precision on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, jax-SNANA simulates more than 100,000 LSST-observed supernovae per second and fits 5,000 light curves per second after JIT compilation, a two orders-of-magnitude increase over current tools, essential for analysing samples at the scale expected from LSST. jax-SNANA currently supports the SALT and BayeSN spectral energy distribution (SED) models as well as physical models from redback-jax and a variety of SN SED templates; light curve fitting is supported with both photometric and spectroscopic redshifts. We fully validate the accuracy of jax-SNANA by comparing to SNANA, finding excellent consistency between the two across a variety of tasks. The code provides a modular JAX end-to-end supernova cosmology pipeline, user-extensible to support new features including different SED templates and photometric classification algorithms. jax-SNANA has been designed with future applications of simulation-based inference in mind, providing fast simulations and enabling fully compiled on-the-fly simulations to be generated within the training loop of downstream SBI tasks. jax-SNANA extends beyond SNANA by supporting simulations of generic SN-host galaxy relationships and multiple sub-populations of events, for example originating from young and old progenitors. jax-SNANA is publicly available at https://github.com/mattgrayling/jax-snana and installable through pip.

title: The convective-transition gap in 47 Tucanae with JWST
comment: 9 pages, 10 figures (6 in Appendices A-E), 2 tables (1 in Appendix A). Accepted for publication in A&A Letters on 6 October 2026. Manuscript ID: aa61668-26
summary: We report the detection of the convective-transition gap along the lower main sequence (MS) of the Galactic globular cluster (GC) 47 Tucanae using deep James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations. We analyse the stellar luminosity function (LF) in the vicinity of the gap location using two independent colour-magnitude diagrams (CMDs). In both cases, the LF is characterised by a narrow gap followed by a discontinuous increase in the stellar number counts, and presents an overall morphology qualitatively consistent with that reported in previous studies. By modelling the observed LFs with an empirical likelihood model, we estimate the statistical significance of the observed feature. Additional JWST passbands exhibit similar signatures, providing further evidence for the presence of a discontinuity.

title: The mass functions of multiple stellar populations in 47 Tucanae
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures (3 in Appendices A-B), 1 table in Appendix A. Published in A&A Letters (https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202661178). Accepted on 8 July 2026
summary: We used a combination of James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and Hubble Space Telescope (HST) observations to investigate the mass functions (MFs) of the different stellar populations in the globular cluster (GC) 47 Tucanae (NGC 104) over a wide stellar-mass interval. We identified the multiple populations along the lower main sequence using only JWST photometry and, in particular, colour combinations sensitive to variations in oxygen abundance. We derived the MFs of the first- and second-population (1P and 2P) stars separately and found that in the low-mass regime, the present-day MF of the 1P population is significantly steeper than that of the 2P population, which appears nearly flat. We also present the results of a dynamical model showing that this behaviour requires a different initial mass function (IMF) for the 2P and the 1P populations in the 0.1-0.4 solar masses mass range, thus providing a new fundamental constraint for the study of the star formation of multiple populations in GCs.

title: JWST observations of 47 Tucanae: I. The low-mass main sequence down to the hydrogen-burning limit
comment: 16 pages, 14 figures (1 figure in Appendix A), 1 table. Published in A&A (https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202660362). Accepted on 22 June 2026
summary: We present the first results of a series of studies based on JWST observations of the globular cluster 47 Tucanae (47 Tuc, or NGC 104) obtained with NIRCam. By combining new data with earlier JWST observations, we derive high-precision proper motions (PMs) over a multi-year baseline (of ~3 years) and construct a clean sample of cluster members extending to very faint magnitudes (F444W~24.25 mag, corresponding to ~0.077 solar masses, slightly above the estimated hydrogen-burning limit of 47 Tuc, ~0.074 solar masses) along the main sequence (MS). We investigated the presence of the low-mass MS kink previously identified in 47 Tuc using the new F090W and F444W photometry. No significant signature of the feature is found using these filters, consistent with its proposed physical interpretation as a consequence of the transition in carbon chemistry toward a methane-dominated equilibrium in very low-mass stars. A comparison with theoretical isochrones indicates that the stellar population near the bottom of the MS is likely dominated by oxygen-poor stars, in agreement with previous findings. Using artificial-star tests, we quantify the completeness of our sample and show that the requirement of PM-based membership significantly limits the detection of the faintest objects, indicating that current JWST observations of 47 Tuc are not sufficiently deep to reliably trace the cluster's brown dwarf cooling sequence. The mass function (MF) of 47 Tuc shows a structured behaviour, with a break at ~0.15 solar masses not associated with the onset of convection, and a mild but systematic radial variation consistent with mass segregation. Our analysis indicates that the MF shape in this mass regime is more complex than a simple power-law description. This feature in the MF may point to a presently unrecognised mechanism affecting the formation or dynamical evolution of low-mass stars in globular clusters.

title: Audible curvaton: modulated phase transition as the origin of large-scale curvature perturbations and gravitational wave anisotropies
comment: 12 pages, 1 figure
summary: We propose a post-inflationary first-order phase transition modulated by a light spectator field as the origin of primordial large-scale curvature perturbations. Spectator fluctuations acquired during inflation modulate the bubble nucleation history, generating curvature perturbations together with correlated intrinsic gravitational-wave (GW) anisotropies. We show that this mechanism can reproduce the observed amplitude of curvature perturbations while producing a loud stochastic GW background in the frequency bands of space-based detectors such as LISA, Taiji, and TianQin. A concrete benchmark yields strongly enhanced intrinsic GW anisotropies and a local primordial non-Gaussianity signal within reach of future large-scale-structure surveys.

title: Enabling Polyspectra via Stochastic Realizations of Inverse Decay Curvature Perturbations in Axion Inflation
summary: Current and upcoming galaxy-redshift surveys offer a promising path for constraining inflationary physics. These constraints are often imposed by relating correlations of the primordial curvature perturbation to the late-time galaxy correlation functions. The primordial correlators can either be computed analytically, or via realizations of the primordial curvature perturbations that are initialized on a grid and evolved numerically according to the classical equations of motion. In this work we take a hybrid approach, initializing the fields in the Bunch-Davies vacuum; and then imposing time evolution through direct numerical integration. Our method efficiently generates realizations of the inverse decay primordial curvature perturbations for axion inflation---an inflationary model in which a pseudoscalar inflaton field couples to a $U(1)$ gauge field via a Chern-Simons interaction. Depending on the choice of parameter $ξ\in\{2, 2.5, 3\}$, which controls gauge field particle production in this model, our method generates realizations with an average runtime of a few hours on 1 CPU core. We compute the power spectrum and bispectrum from these realizations and find a surprisingly large discrepancy between our result and previous work that used an approximation for the gauge field mode functions---up to a factor of $\sim4$ difference for the bispectrum in the case of $ξ=2$. This new method enables not only rapid computation of higher order polyspectra, but also generation of initial conditions for large-scale structure analyses.

title: Testing the 4-Point Correlation Function as a Probe of Parity Violation with the Quijote-Odd Simulations
comment: 11 Pages, 3 figures
summary: We investigate parity violation searches with the 4-Point Correlation Function (4PCF) using the Quijote and Quijote-Odd halo catalogs. Specifically, we explore the auto- and cross-correlation searching methodologies that have been previously used in the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) and the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) searches. Although the Quijote-Odd simulations are initialized with a parity-violating primordial trispectrum, we find no statistically detectable parity-odd signal in the halo 4PCF. Instead, we find that the halo measurements are dominated by Poisson noise. We are able to distinguish this noise-dominated behavior from the response expected for a parity-odd signal. These results clarify how parity-sensitive 4PCF statistics respond to noise in a controlled simulation setting.

title: Dynamical formation of dormant black holes: Predictions for Gaia DR4
comment: 13 pages, 10 figures, submitted to A&A
summary: Dormant black holes (dormant BHs, i.e., X-ray quiet binaries comprising a BH and a companion star) are probes of the effect of cluster dynamics and binary stellar evolution on compact-object binaries. A dozen dormant BH binaries are known, a number that will increase substantially with the upcoming Gaia Data Release 4 (DR4). Their origin is uncertain, and dynamical formation is proposed as one possible channel. Here, we study the formation of dormant BHs in low-mass star clusters, accounting for the interplay of binary stellar evolution and cluster dynamics. We present new simulations with the $N$-body code PeTar, interfaced with the population synthesis code SEVN for single and binary star evolution. Our grid spans a range of cluster masses ($300-4800\,$M$_\odot$), metallicities ($1.4\times10^{-2}$, $1.4\times10^{-4}$), and natal kick models (with and without fallback). We find that almost all dormant BH binaries escape the parent cluster within $\sim1\,$Gyr ($\sim10\,$Myr) when assuming weak (strong) natal kicks. Most ($73\%$) dormant BHs form via the exchange of a BH (or its progenitor star) into a stellar binary, or of a star into a binary with a BH. Dormant BHs in low-mass clusters have a wide orbital period distribution (from a few hours to $10^8\,$d), with an upper limit set by natal kicks, a bimodal eccentricity distribution (a first peak at zero eccentricity for circularised systems and a second at high eccentricity), and stellar masses that follow the (evolved) initial mass function. Large BH masses are a smoking gun of dynamical formation, via exchanges and stellar collisions. We expect Gaia DR4 to contain $\sim1-64$ high-metallicity and $\sim0.4-48$ low-metallicity dormant BHs, with a period distribution peaking at $\sim10^3\,$d, $\gtrsim90\%$ of them with eccentricity $e>0.1$, and $\sim20\%$ with large BH masses ($m_{\rm BH} \gtrsim 30\,$M$_\odot$).

title: Broadband non-thermal emission predictions based on 3D simulations of supernova explosions within active galactic nuclei jets
summary: Thermonuclear and core-collapse supernovae are statistically expected to happen within extragalactic jets, as these jets cross the inner regions of their host galaxies, and supernova ejecta-jet interactions can potentially lead to strong non-thermal activity. We model the non-thermal emission from a supernova interacting with a jet on kiloparsec scales, using detailed numerical simulations of the interaction. Using a post-processing method, we applied a non-thermal model of the acceleration and transport of electron and their synchrotron and inverse Compton emissions, simplified and tuned for flexibility and computational speed, to the results of a three-dimensional relativistic hydrodynamics simulation of the ejecta of a supernova interacting with an extragalactic jet. For intermediate jet powers, radio, optical and X-ray fluxes from supernova ejecta-jet interactions may be detectable for distances < 100Mpc. The non-thermal luminosity budget and local conditions associated with these interactions could be enough to explain knots seen in kiloparsec scale jets at different energies. These conditions might also be suitable for the production of heavy ultra high-energy cosmic rays, but photon and neutrino generation from hadronic processes would be minor on kiloparsec scales. The leptonic gamma-ray fluxes are modest but might non-negligibly contribute in TeV for the nearest or more powerful jet sources.

title: EDGE-INFERNO: The chemical signatures of assembly history in reionization fossils
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. Abstract abridged for arXiv
summary: In galaxies, stellar populations represent a superposition of both in situ and accreted components, tracing internal chemical evolution as well as the histories of merged satellites. We investigate how assembly history shapes the chemical properties of present-day stellar populations in low-mass dwarf galaxies. We analyze a suite of EDGE-INFERNO star-by-star cosmological zoom-in simulations of galaxies with present-day halo mass $\sim1.4\times10^9\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$. We systematically vary galaxy growth while preserving the present-day halo mass, engineering our simulations to span a continuum of assembly histories. Early-forming systems form most of their stars in a single progenitor, with centrally concentrated star formation and a continuous enrichment history. In contrast, our late-forming systems assemble by accretion of multiple progenitors with their own stellar populations, resulting in fragmented star formation across several halos with independent chemical evolution tracks. These regimes produce qualitatively different chemical signatures: single-progenitor systems exhibit connected, well-defined trends in abundance space, while multi-progenitor systems show multiple, distinct stellar populations with limited overlap. We find that metallicity distribution functions provide initial constraints on assembly history for samples of at least $50$-$100$ member stars. Multi-element abundance analysis significantly improves the recovery of distinct components, although robust reconstruction still requires larger samples. Fully separating in situ and accreted populations likely requires kinematic information. Accreted stars can contribute substantially even at high metallicities in multi-progenitor systems, while external enrichment can cause accreted material to follow similar chemical trends as in situ stars, particularly in the single-progenitor regime.

title: Cosmological Consequences of a Highly Decoupled Right-handed Neutrino
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures, 1 table. Comments are welcome
summary: In the minimal type-I seesaw, one right-handed neutrino (RHN) can decouple from neutrino mass generation. Such a state is usually neglected, yet its feeble couplings make it long-lived, and it can dominate the energy density of the Universe before decaying. We study this in a minimal $U(1)_{B-L}$ model, where the RHNs are produced through $B-L$ gauge interactions, for the cases of a decoupled lightest RHN $N_1$ and a decoupled heaviest RHN $N_3$. The resulting early matter-dominated era dilutes the baryon asymmetry, and for decoupled $N_3$ it also delays the equilibration of the charged-lepton Yukawa interactions, allowing a lighter $N_1$ to generate the asymmetry in the unflavoured regime. Breaking $U(1)_{B-L}$ forms cosmic strings whose gravitational-wave background acquires a spectral break from the early matter-dominated era, with a frequency set by the decoupled RHN mass and the lightest neutrino mass, within reach of future detectors such as SKA, THEIA, LISA, $μ$ARES, DECIGO and ET.

title: Validation of harmonic-space likelihood methods for LiteBIRD B-mode polarisation analysis
comment: 42 pages, 17 figures, prepared for the submission to JCAP
summary: The LiteBIRD satellite mission aims to measure the tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$ with unprecedented sensitivity through observations of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) $B$-mode polarisation. Robust constraints on $r$ require accurate likelihood modelling across a wide range of angular scales. In this work, we validate harmonic-space likelihood methods against pixel-based benchmarks using 20\,000 end-to-end simulations that include CMB, instrumental noise, and Galactic foreground residuals processed through a realistic component-separation pipeline. We compare a debiased pixel-based likelihood, which serves as our benchmark on large scales ($\ell\leq32$), with an offset Hamimeche \& Lewis (oHL) likelihood applicable across the full multipole range. We systematically explore the space of analysis settings, identifying the number of simulations used for covariance estimation and the choice of beam window function as the most critical factors. Over the full multipole range considered ($\ell\leq128$), where the benchmark combines the pixel-based likelihood at $\ell\leq32$ with a harmonic one at smaller scales, the 68\% upper bound on $r$ from the oHL likelihood is $19$--$29\%$ larger than the benchmark one, depending on the beam window function. This demonstrates its viability as a computationally efficient baseline for LiteBIRD data analysis and cosmological inference from the polarisation $B$-mode field.

title: IC 1297: The Most Distant Known X-ray Planetary Nebula and One of the Most Luminous
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: We present the first targeted Einstein Probe (EP) X-ray observations of any planetary nebula (PN). Using the onboard Follow-up X-ray Telescope (FXT), we detect X-ray emission within the central region of IC 1297. The spectral analysis yields a plasma temperature of $kT = 0.086^{+0.054}_{-0.058}$ keV ($T\sim1.0 \times 10^{6}$ K), characteristic of shocked wind bubbles in PNe, whereas there is no evidence that its Wolf-Rayet central star emits X-rays. The absorption-corrected X-ray luminosity in the 0.3--2.0 keV energy band is $L_{\mathrm{X}} = 2.8 \times 10^{32}$ erg s$^{-1}$, also consistent with a hot bubble. At an adopted distance of $\sim3.8$ kpc, IC 1297 is the most distant X-ray emitting PN found to date, opening up a new observational window on hot-bubble formation and evolution. It is also among the most luminous known X-ray-emitting PNe. Our results demonstrate the capability of the EP FXT for detecting and characterizing faint, extended X-ray sources in the soft X-ray band for distant PNe, extending the known spectral properties of detectable X-ray emitting PNe. We also compiled the X-ray properties of all 41 known Galactic XPNe, finding a clear correlation between distance and X-ray luminosity that reflects an observational bias toward detecting the brightest sources at large distances. The compilation also shows a separation in X-ray luminosity between hot bubbles powered by H-rich and [WR]-type central stars, with the latter reaching luminosities up to an order of magnitude higher. The ten most luminous XPNe all host [WR]/PG 1159 central stars.

title: Enhancing dark siren cosmology via Gaussian process reconstruction of incomplete galaxy catalogs
comment: 16 pages, 11 figures
summary: We present a novel framework for improving dark siren cosmology by applying a Gaussian process (GP) to the line-of-sight (LOS) reconstruction of incomplete galaxy catalogs. In the standard galaxy catalog method for inferring the Hubble constant $H_0$ from gravitational-wave (GW) dark sirens, missing galaxies are typically assumed to follow a uniform distribution in comoving volume, an assumption that discards galaxy redshift clustering information crucial for cosmological inference. We propose instead to model the LOS galaxy redshift distribution as a non-parametric function drawn from a GP realization, which is fitted to the observed incomplete catalog via a hierarchical Bayesian likelihood that explicitly accounts for the survey selection function. Applied to mock GW and galaxy catalogs extending up to redshift $z\leq0.4$, our method yields $H_0$ constraints that are on average 23% more precise than the standard homogeneous completion when using a 24%-complete galaxy catalog, and 37% more precise for an 8%-complete catalog. The largest improvement, reaching 66%, is obtained in configurations where the GP most effectively reconstructs the redshift over- and under-density features that the homogeneous completion fails to capture.

title: Memoirs of the curvaton: non-perturbative non-Gaussianity and supermassive primordial black holes
comment: 39 pages, 12 figures + Appendix. Matches the version published in JCAP
summary: The curvaton provides a simple mechanism for generating strongly non-Gaussian curvature perturbations after inflation, with potentially important consequences on small scales. We study curvaton dynamics beyond the standard quadratic potential and construct the local non-Gaussian map $ζ=F(ζ_{\rm G})$ relating the curvature perturbation to an auxiliary Gaussian field $ζ_{\rm G}$. Curvaton self-interactions make the onset of oscillations field dependent and modify the effective equation of state once the curvaton enters the adiabatic regime. We incorporate these effects using the abbreviated action, which provides a compact way to connect the frozen and oscillatory regimes and exposes sources of non-Gaussianity absent in the purely quadratic case. We apply the formalism to quadratic, monomial, quartic, and cosine potentials, for which we derive the mapping $F(ζ_{\rm G})$ and show that self-interactions can either enhance or suppress the resulting non-Gaussianity depending on the potential and initial conditions. We consider non-perturbative aspects in the strongly non-Gaussian regime, and show how strong non-Gaussianity can suppress the power spectrum. As an application, we provide a bottom-up scenario in which strongly positive curvaton non-Gaussianity allows primordial supermassive black hole seeds at peak amplitudes $\mathcal{A}_{\rm pk}\sim10^{-5}$, which are compatible with the COBE/FIRAS $μ$-distortion bounds. This opens a new primordial scenario for the Little Red Dots observed by the JWST. The axion-like curvaton provides a particularly natural setting for this mechanism.
